On March 29, Le Soleil of Quebec reported as follows part of a speech I had made the previous day:
Every speech has been a funeral oration for the United Nations which was given a first class funeral. The member for Argenteuil talked at great length on national sovereignty. What is national sovereignty? It is a square wheel. It is incomprehensible that an intelligent lawyer like Mr. Heon should speak about national sovereignty as he has done.
Here is what I said, Mr. Speaker, as reported on page 2103 of Hansard:
I heard the member for Argenteuil (Mr. Heon) speak a little while ago. He talked about national sovereignty. Whoever thought of that? It is a square wheel; it is nonsense. I cannot understand such a brilliant lawyer using that expression. It shows how-I will not use the word "silly"-strange some people can be in their reasoning when they begin to talk on matters that they know nothing about.
(Text):
I was referring, Mr. Speaker, to an erroneous report which had been made of a speech which I delivered on March 28 in reply to the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Heon).

rise now, Mr. Speaker, on a special question of privilege by virtue of standing order 16 and standing order 41, which deal with the use of abusive language in reference to members of parliament. In Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, there are several citations dealing with the privileges and immunities of members of parliament, and I would draw your attention to citations 151, 153 and 157. Citation 157 reads:
Interference with or reflections upon members have been resented as indignities to the house itself. May, 79.
Among the expressions that have been ruled to be unparliamentary in the British House of Commons is the adverb "cowardly". The adjective "coward" has the same meaning, and is just as objectionable. Let me refer you to the latest edition of Campion's Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons; I quote from page 71 as follows:
Attempts to threaten or intimidate members for their actions in the house have been declared to be breaches of privilege by the house, and offenders have been punished in numerous instances by reprimand or imprisonment. Libels on members have also been constantly punished, but they cannot be raised as breaches of privilege if they concern a member in any other respect than his conduct in the house.
Questions of privilege refer to the conduct of a member of parliament in the house in the fulfilment of his parliamentary duties. Paragraph 8 on page 194 refers to May, where is to be found a list of expressions to which exception has been taken at various times. I would refer also to Bourinot at page 361 and following. At page 363 it says that it is a breach of privilege to impute want of courage to a member of parliament. I also have the fourteenth edition of May, and I refer to pages 102, 103, 431, 432'and 441. At page 441 there is a paragraph entitled "the use of disorderly or unparliamentary words."
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I now come to the question of privilege proper. I have been a member of parliament for nearly twenty-five years.
And a good member of parliament.

In my long career I have no knowledge of an anonymous letter being sent to any member of parliament by one of his colleagues. It may seem strange, but the envelope is a House of Commons envelope. It was mailed at the House of Commons post office, and is stamped with the House of Commons stamp, including the date, March 28. It is addressed to "G."-for George-F. " Poulio," M.P., "Temiscouta, H. of Commons." There is no frank. If there were a frank it would not be an anonymous letter.
This is the letter, which is on House of Commons paper. I think it was Shakespeare who said, "He jests at scars that never felt a wound." This letter is an insult to every member of the House of Commons, on account of the two letters "M.P." as the signature

Privilege
at the bottom of it. I shall read the letter. I do not know who sent it to me. I have been on good terms with all my colleagues, but I consider that this letter is unique in my long experience as a member of parliament.
The letter reads as follows:
House of Commons Canada

A man who is not yellow-
And "yellow" is underlined twice.
-and has the courage of his convictions should stay in the house and vote. You gave the impression of a coward who runs away in the face of danger. You are not a Liberal but a jackal, and we are ashamed of you I

Of course, Mr. Speaker, jackals feed on carrion, small animals and poultry. It is a sign of a certain degree of modesty on the part of the writer of the anonymous letter. I will send you, Mr. Speaker, the envelope and the letter as soon as the official reporters have copied it. I hope that Your Honour will investigate this incident, which is unique, and take whatever action Your Honour may deem to be necessary under the circumstances.

May I say to the hon. member for Temiscouata that I have noted his remarks, and, if it is deemed necessary, after due consideration, the whole constabulary force of the House of Commons will be put on the alert to find the guilty party.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ONTARIO

speechtext: On the order for motions:

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ONTARIO
speechtext:
I have pleasure in informing the house that an agreement has just been signed with the province of Ontario under the provisions of the National Physical Fitness Act, 1943. This agreement has been signed by Hon. Dana Porter, provincial minister of education, on behalf of the province of Ontario, and by myself on behalf of the federal government.
Under this act the federal government provides financial assistance to the provinces annually to assist them in the development of their physical fitness and recreation programs. This amount is divided on a per capita basis among the various provinces. Ontario's maximum share under this formula amounts to $74,063.25 annually. The federal grant matches provincial expenditures dollar for dollar up to this maximum.
The signing of this agreement with the province of Ontario brings to eight the number of provinces which are now co-operating with the dominion government in a physical fitness and recreation program. British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have been carrying on programs under the National Physical Fitness Act since 1944. New Brunswick and the Northwest Territories entered into agreements for the first time in 1947. This leaves the province of Quebec as the only province under the National Physical Fitness Act which has not yet entered into an agreement with the federal government to take advantage of the financial provisions of the act.
I should of course add that an agreement can be entered into between Newfoundland and the federal government under the Statute Law Amendment Act.

subtopic: STRIKE OF CANADIAN SEAMEN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STRIKE OF CANADIAN SEAMEN
speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Will the minister give the house a report on the shipping strike which now has tied up deep-sea shipping on the Pacific as well as the Atlantic coast? May I say that this is important, and that the members of the house as well as the people of the country should have a factual report on the situation.

subtopic: STRIKE OF CANADIAN SEAMEN
speechtext:
I expected someone would ask me this question today, so I have come prepared to answer it.
For some months the dispute involving unlicensed personnel employed by the Canadian deep-sea shipping companies has been receiving the attention of the Department of Labour under the conciliation procedure laid down by parliament in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
Late last September I was advised that the shipowners and the Canadian seamen's union had been unable to arrive at any settlement in their negotiations for a renewal of their collective agreement, which was due to expire on October 15, 1948. I appointed a conciliation officer, who held a number of conferences with the parties but was unable to reconcile the differences between them. Following receipt of the conciliation officer's report I appointed a board of conciliation and investigation, under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice J. O. Wilson, of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, the other members of

Inquiries of the Ministry the board being Theodore Meighen, K.C., of Montreal, nominated by the shipowners, and John Kerry, K.C., also of Montreal, nominated by the union.
The conciliation board conducted an exhaustive investigation into all the matters in dispute, and held extensive public hearings in Montreal. Finding that it was unable to effect a settlement, the board reported to me in February. The report of the board was unanimous, and was accompanied by a draft agreement which the board recommended for execution by the shipowners and the union.
The shipowners subsequently advised me that they were prepared to accept the recommendations of the conciliation board, but the union rejected the board's recommendations, stating that the recommended hiring arrangements would bring about a chaotic condition and that the over-all effect of the proposed agreement would involve a reduction in the take-home pay of the seamen. The union proposed that further conferences with the shipowners be held.
I might remind hon. members that under the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act the prohibitions against the parties as to strikes or lockouts are no longer in effect seven days after the receipt of the conciliation board's report.
About ten days ago the Canadian seamen's union adopted a new procedure, that of having the seamen refuse to sign new sailing articles, thus preventing the ships from sailing. Delays have occurred to several ships, including some Canadian National steamships. Since that time the officers of my department-and when I say the officers of my department I include myself-have kept in close touch with developments on the east coast, and have made it known to the parties that the conciliation services of the department would be available to them at any time.
On Thursday of last week, at the request of Mr. Percy R. Bengough, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the deputy minister of labour and the director of industrial relations of the labour department met a delegation consisting of Mr. Bengough and Messrs. Harry Davis and T. G. McManus, president and secretary of the Canadian seamen's union. The conversations were of an exploratory nature, and were discontinued late that afternoon when it was learned that the seafarers international union of North America had entered into an agreement with the east coast shipowners. ,
The department has been advised by a number of shipowners that they have received

a letter from Mr. Joseph P. Ryan, president of the international longshoremen's association, in the following terms:
You are aware of the controversy involving the Canadian seamen's union, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the American Federation of Labor, and a number of affiliated A.F. of L. organizations.
This situation is giving cause for grave concern to a number of international unions, including those engaged in the shipping and maritime industry. Among these is the longshoremen's association, which is anxious to see that this controversy is disposed of in such a way as to eliminate those communist elements which have kept the industry in an unsettled condition for so long.
We would be disturbed if your company continued to give aid and comfort to the communist group, particularly the Canadian seamen's union, and we feel that we should advise you of this so that our own relations and operations may be continued on an amicable basis.
And a subsequent telegram from Mr. Ryan reading as follows:
Please advise if you are now in a position to assure me crews on your vessels will not come under domination of communists in order that loading and unloading instructions may be given my people.
That reference is to unloading instructions in the United States.
These communications may have an indirect bearing on the owners' consideration of the matter. Advices from Halifax are to the effect that: (a) Canadian members of Mr. Ryan's organization at Halifax and Saint John are respecting the picket lines of the Canadian seamen's union; (b) members of the Canadian seamen's union have left the C.N.R. vessel upon being served with a court order to do so; (c) there have been no disturbances at these ports.

maintopic: REPORTED UNEMPLOYMENT AT HEAD OF THE LAKES

maintopic: REPORTED UNEMPLOYMENT AT HEAD OF THE LAKES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can make a statement to the house. It is a simple one. Anyone who has any knowledge of the head of the lakes knows that at the moment there is a seasonal fluctuation of labour there. Men are coming out of the woods, and they will be going back. I make this prediction, notwithstanding the calamity howlers: this will be the greatest year of productive effort this nation has ever seen.

-a full statement ... as to any additional consideration now being given fanners with regard to the allowance for depreciation on the farm house, because of the preponderant part it plays in the farm business; and also as to the basis on which it is to be calculated.
My answer is this: In view of the large part which the farm home plays in the conduct of the farm business, it has been decided that commencing in 1948 a farmer who resides on the farm may claim depreciation on the cost of the farm house at one-quarter of the usual rate of depreciation, and may also claim one-quarter of the cost of repairs to the house, in addition to the full amount of the cost for light, power, taxes, telephone and fire insurance. Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to discuss a matter which I could not bring up on the orders of the day because it requires some explanation. I do not want to delay the house too long, but I think the time has come when we should get from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) a statement of the government's policy with respect to national health insurance. The house and the country need to know, by means of a categorical statement, whether the government of Canada is in favour of national health insurance or not. If it is in favour of national health insurance, when is it going to take the initiative in bringing it about?
I know of course that a great deal has been made of the relatively inadequate health grants which have been made available to the provinces over the last year or so; but it seems to me that if we are to have a real health plan in Canada we should not rely upon a system of that kind. We should have a definite bill before us so that an act of parliament governing national health insurance could be put on the statute book.
I bring this question before the house because there are rumours that a federal election is in the air.
Do you believe that?

Whether I believe it or not, I tell the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) that rumours are in the air. During the last general election, in 1945, a great deal of attention was paid to national health insurance, by gentlemen who occupy seats on the government side, and their supporters. In 1944 a draft bill was introduced into this chamber and received first reading. A draft bill was before the social security committee of the House of Commons and was thoroughly gone into. I remember that in 1945 this bill was placed before the electors in printed form. It was taken up and down the country, and the people were told: This is the bill that the government intends to do something with if it is re-elected. I have heard nothing of the bill since. It was a very important measure, so important that a great deal of attention was paid to it.
I note that the committee on social security of that time heard 117 witnesses, representing thirty-two groups, including the health insurance committees which had

appeared before the advisory committee on health insurance. All groups expressed themselves generally in favour of the principle of health insurance. After discussing the draft bill the special committee on social security made the following report to this House of Commons:
The committee approves of the general principles of health insurance set forth in the health insurance bill respecting public health, health insurance, the prevention of disease and other -matters related thereto.
If hon. members will look at the bills- and I use the plural-which were discussed at that time, they will find that a most comprehensive plan of health insurance was indeed approved by that committee and placed before the house, and,- as I say, it was printed and discussed across the country.
Those of us who are much interested in this type of legislation have been waiting for a statement from the government and from the minister as to what the present intention is with respect to the recommendations made by that committee several years ago.
As I remember the bill-and I looked it up-the draft bill and the sample bill which was attached to it covered medical, dental, pharmaceutical, hospital, nursing and all the other services required in illness. Many of our people thought that it was going to be put into effect. Indeed, in my own province of Saskatchewan something of that kind has been put into effect. It was done because the provincial government believed that it would receive some aid in carrying out a general health plan, or that this would become a part of a general health plan for Canada. They have been disappointed.
I want to find out what is the government's policy in regard to this matter now. I repeat that grants by order in council are uncertain and unsatisfactory. If we are to have a national health plan which will meet the needs of the Canadian people, it has to be on a dominion-wide basis. It is true it will have to be by provincial administration, but it should be in the form of a statute and not by way of estimates and orders in council. What I want to find out is if the idea has been abandoned; because I have been looking up newspapers, and I find, for example, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) spoke in Toronto on April 1, and in the course of that speech he recalled a recent statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in which the Prime Minister said:
It is up to the people and the government in each province to take the initiative in working out health insurance plans in line with their local conditions and their traditions.
National Health Insurance
Then my hon. friend himself commented:
Canada, through such measures as the Atlantic security pact, was building bastions around its way of life, but must not fail the cause of humanity by slackening up the drive forward towards social justice.
How thoroughly I agree with that! But what I am pointing out is that the government appears to have slowed up the pace in matters of social justice. The minister goes on:
If this nation is to withstand the pressures of other political philosophies, Canadians must continue to shape up in this country measures for the health and welfare of our people that no other country can surpass.
We are a long way from shaping up in our country measures which no other country can surpass. I have been disappointed in what I have read. I have before me a copy of an article which appeared in the Washington Post in January of this year, and I have the page. This article was written by a gentleman who is opposed to the national health plans proposed in the United States by the present president. I refer to Dr. Graham L. Davis, who is the director of the division of hospitals, W. K. Kellogg Foundation, of Battle Creek, Michigan. Dr. Davis had been in Canada. May I just say that he had taken back with him a picture of the Canadian scene in regard to health, and I have learned from the premier of Saskatchewan that the references to Saskatchewan in this report are inaccurate. I am not going to comment on that reference or the report on that province, but I want to refer to this gentleman's impression of the minister and the department over which he presides. Dr. Davis writes:
My impression, gained from conversations with Paul Martin, Minister of National Health and Welfare, and Dr. G, D. W. Cameron, deputy minister of national health, and from participation in a recent three-day conference at Ottawa, is that Canada is not nearly as certain now as it was in 1945 that the compulsory health insurance proposals were the best answer to the problem of financial medical care. For this and other reasons, Canada in 1948 adopted a different approach.
Of course it was a different approach-an approach, incidentally, which is altogether different from the approach in the United States, and in Great Britain, where a scheme has gone into effect which, unpopular with certain sections of the country a year ago, is now generally regarded as the most popular piece of legislation that the government has placed upon the statute books.
In yesterday's Montreal Gazette I noticed an article by Clifton Daniel of the New York

National Health Insurance Times service, in which he discusses the health plans in Great Britain. He says this:
A prospective Conservative candidate for parliament acknowledged that the health service was the most popular measure enacted by the Labour administration, and that one of the major problems of the Conservative policy was how to make legitimate criticisms of the operations and costs of the service without seeming to attack its objectives.
Unpopular among some people a year ago, but today probably the most popular thing that the Labour government has done, is the British national health and medical plan. Similar in many respects, but not in all, to what has been done in Great Britain is the plan now before the congress of the United States which was proposed by the President during the United States elections last November. The bill now before the United States congress creates a national health insurance board within the federal security agency with an administrative set-up-part state, part federal-similar to that of the social security board. It would extend complete medical, dental, hospital and nursing care to everyone except the destitute, who would remain as charity cases. That seems to me to be a strange provision, that the people who are perhaps least able to pay and to care for themselves should be left to charitable organizations. In this it differs from the United Kingdom plan.
Doctors and hospitals could join the plan or not, as they chose. Patients would choose their own doctors, and doctors could reject them if they wished. The medical bills would be paid by the national health insurance board. Doctors would be reimbursed on a stated-fee basis varied to compensate for skills, locations and other differentials. The plan would be financed by a three per cent pay-roll tax. Of course a pay-roll tax is the poorest way to finance a measure of that description. If we are going to have a levy it should be one based on the ability of the person to bear the load. I think that is the point of view we should adopt in that regard.
While the legislation in Great Britain was unpopular in some quarters a year ago, it is now the most popular piece of legislation that the Labour government of Great Britain has put into effect. Since we have been getting so much propaganda against what is going on in Great Britain, propaganda against this health plan, propaganda that is absolutely ill-founded and false, I should like to read parts of an interview that was given by three outstanding medical men of Great Britain while in the United States recently, men who up to a year ago were in the main opposed to the British health plan.
I looked up these doctors in the 1948 British medical directory and anyone who cares to consult the directory will find that while
tMr. Coldwell.]
there are some hundreds of doctors listed these three gentlemen are among the most outstanding in their fields in the United Kingdom.
Sir Stanford Cade, K.B.E., C.B., holds many distinguished offices. He is a member of the executive of the investigating committee of the British empire cancer committee, and so on. Dr. Brian Windeyer is a professor of radiology at London university. He is the author of a number of treatises on cancer, et cetera. Dr. Alexander Haddow is a man of such world-wide reputation that one does not need to look him up in the medical directory. He is a professor of experimental pathology at the university of London, director of the Chester Beatty Research Institute, Royal Cancer Hospital, and so on.
A short time ago these gentlemen were in Memphis, Tennessee, attending the meeting of the American cancer society. At that time they were interviewed by Dr. Edward H. Skinner of Kansas City, Missouri, the editor of the Kansas City southwest clinical society's bulletin and also a leader in the national physicians' committee which is vigorously opposing national health insurance in the United States as well as the President's plan and any other plan which is for state aid in this connection.
Apparently Dr. Skinner had met at least one of these gentlemen in Great Britain last year and he thought he would find some good grist for his mill, some good ammunition to use against the health plan which is proposed in the United States and which is similar in some respects to that in effect in Great Britain. Sir Stanford Cade and Dr. Brian W. Windeyer were interviewed by Dr. Skinner and I should like to read a few extracts from the report of that interview as it appeared in the Kansas City Star:-
"What is the effect on the income and social status of English doctors?"
"Fine," said Sir Stanford.
"Fine?" Doctor Skinner said, as if his ears heard wrong.	.
"Fine," repeated Sir Stanford, and he leaned forward. "More patients, more income."
This is not what Sir Stanford had predicted of the health scheme he had opposed so vigorously during Doctor Skinner's 1947 visit to England.
"Exactly," said Sir Stanford, "it hasn't worked out as I feared. I must tell you frankly, the doctors of England are being disillusioned in a pleasant way.
We still have our essential freedom. We have more work, more pay. And the people, I am sure, are getting better medical care."
"But the cost, Sir Stanford, the cost," said the Kansas City citizen, hitching up his chair, while Doctor Joseph L. Farrow of New York, his son-inlaw, watched.
Sir Stanford shrugged.
"The cost," he said. "What did the atomic bomb cost? What did the last war cost? Destruction costs billions, so why not some billions for everybody's health, say the people."

Doctor Windeyer nodded at this and said the present government of England was not quaking at the health service cost, and was assuming the service would go on decade after decade, under Labour, Liberal or Conservative party governments.
"What are the results in terms of effectiveness of service to the patient, in office consultations and in hospitals?" was Doctor Skinner's next question.
"Good," said Doctor Windeyer. "The poor see they no longer have to depend on charity for medical care."
"Are the doctors still obligated to visit some patients in their homes?" Doctor Skinner continued.
"If the doctor has signed a contract to give them service-yes," was the answer.
"Is a patient allowed to transfer from one doctor to another-has he free choice of a physician?" "The patient has this choice, and the doctor, too, has the right not to continue to treat a patient if he feels results are not what they should be," Doctor Windeyer replied
"How does it affect hospital morale, and nursing services?" Doctor Skinner went on.
"The pay of nurses has been doubled," Doctor Windeyer said.
"Isn't there a lack of enterprise and initiative on the part of doctors? If they have a stipulated income from each patient, paid by the government, why should they seek to give improved service or seek out better ways?"
"Doctor Skinner," said Sir Stanford in response to these questions, "we are finding that the standard of care the doctor gives is as good as under the private enterprise method. A man is inherently honest and a seeker of better wavs toward health, or he isn't. That applies to different doctors in either type of service.
"I would suggest," Sir Stanford continued, "that the American doctor welcome any plan of medical service to all, projected in America. Let the doctor go into it and give the leadership.
"You have a great and rich country, fine doctors, and when the ground-swell of a national medical service starts, the opportunity is for the doctors more than for the politicians, in the final analysis.
We assume that the people trust competent doctors, under a national medical service or otherwise, and are finding that the doctor more than the politician is the determining factor in the actual control of socialized medicine. So I say to you and other American doctors-when a national health service is wanted, go into it as leaders and planners of a comprehensive enterprise desired by the majority of the people."
Then the other medical man to whom I referred, Dr. Haddow, the great cancer specialist, said something similar. He describes the British health service so far as "an instrument of achievement." I read:
"It holds potential dangers as well as potential benefits," Dr. Haddow said, "and the best policy is the flexible policy, for correcting the errors, compromising the disputes, adjusting the disorders in the administration."
Does the plan not apply to Scotland?

Of course the plan applies there also. I am reading from a United States newspaper, and unfortunately the people of that country usually refer to England, Scotland and Wales as England. If you and I were referring to the same countries we would speak either of the United Kingdom or of Great Britain, but I was reading at the time from a United States news-29087-148J
National Health Insurance paper. This scheme applies to the United Kingdom. I think anyone who has been in the United Kingdom has seen that it is appreciated in that country. I know what my own experience was last autumn in Great Britain. One day traveling on the train I heard a very heated argument between two gentlemen. I discovered afterwards that one of them, the man who was saying that thousands of pairs of spectacles were being distributed to people, and that everybody was getting new dentures, and so on, was a London lawyer. The other man pointed out to him that the people who were getting the spectacles were getting them because they needed them, and were getting new dentures because they needed new dentures. He also added that it was a public scandal that up to this time so many people in Great Britain had been deprived of spectacles and dentures because they could not pay for them. That gentleman is a surgeon. I happen to have his card in my pocket this afternoon.
One was impressed with what was being done in that country to care for those who needed care by way of medical services. In spite of the difficulties, what a wonderful thing it is to have, at least in one great democratic country, without regimentation and by the free vote of the people, a nationwide plan in which everybody participates.
The other day at dinner I heard an American, speaking to my own friends, tell a story which impressed me because a similar thing happened when we arrived at the airport in London. When we arrived there we were given a yellow card, and we were told to hold that yellow card as long as we were in Great. Britain. What did that card do? It gave me, and this American friend who told his story to my friends, the right while we were in Great Britain as visitors to participate in this great scheme. If we needed a doctor we could call one. If we needed a tooth extracted, or something else done to our teeth, we could call a dentist. If we needed! to go into a hospital we could go into a hospital and take advantage of the care that was provided by the people of that country as freely as the people of that country get it today.
The United States are paying for it.

My hon. friend says that the United States are paying for it. I think that kind of remark is beneath the hon. gentleman who made it. I have very great respect for the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), as have all members of the house, but the-hon. member knows that is simply not true. He knows that these medical health services are being paid for by the British people out

National Health Insurance of their sterling funds, of which they have a vast quantity that they cannot use in the dollar area. Because they cannot use them in the dollar area the dollar area has had to assist in the rehabilitation of western Europe and the United Kingdom, not so much because of the United Kingdom itself as because the United Kingdom is the key to rehabilitation in the rest of the world. It is not charity; it is self-defence which has brought the European recovery plan into being.
We should not forget, either, that a short time ago we were in a common war together. In that common war those countries suffered devastation that we escaped. When we, as a part of the rehabilitation of a world which suffered from war, make a contribution to the western European nations, including Great Britain, we are simply assuming a part of the share that we should assume for the rebuilding of this devastated world. As for saying continually that the United States is paying for something, I want to say that the United States is paying for nothing in regard to the medical scheme. I appreciate the generosity of that great country in doing what it is doing for the world, but what the people of Great Britain are doing in this connection for their own social security they are doing with their own sterling funds; they are doing it out of their own resources. We should recognize that.
I am not arguing whether it is being paid ior by the United States, by Great Britain "herself, or by somebody else. What I am arguing is that this great plan which is now in effect in Great Britain, and which is working well, should be an inspiration to the minister and to the government. The minister and the government were talking about national health insurance five years ago, but now they are turning around and saying that the initiative must be taken by the provinces. That is what I am after. I am trying to get the minister and the government to say categorically to the Canadian people that they are going to take the initiative, that they are going to give leadership in the building up of a Canadian national health program that will be available to all our people so that the poorest as well as the richest can get the best medical care, the best hospitalization, the best nursing care, the best pharmaceutical, dental, optical and other facilities that are needed to ensure decent health for the whole nation.
I am keenly interested in this matter. I think that this is the most important project that the government can undertake at this time.
At any time.

At any time. But I am disturbed because bit by bit I have seen the retreat from the proposals of 1944 and 1945 until today, while we get a great deal of talk and a tremendous amount of fanfare across the country, we are not getting the policy that we need. Therefore I am asking that the minister this afternoon make a categorical statement on the matter and let the people of Canada know, not in words, but by the promise to introduce a measure at this session before the election that will lay a real foundation for a medical health plan for all the people of Canada.

have listened with interest to the speech which has been made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) about socialist medicine. He has quoted to us the example of the United Kingdom. I have another example to put before the house in a few words, and it is much nearer to us. I wonder why we should take it for granted that the right must always come from Great Britain because there is a socialist government in power there at the present time.
That is not the reason.
Get a little light from Saskatchewan.
Have your factories not closed down?
Your woollen mill has closed down.
This is not the choice of the British people.
Your factories have closed down.
You have your woollen mills closed down, too.

This is just an observation on the appeal of socialist policies to certain people. I am opposed categorically to compulsory health insurance, for the reason that those who need special care most of the time have not the means to pay for it, and therefore cannot contribute to the fund.
They get it free.
Just a moment; they do not get it free as quickly as that.
They get it free now.
Just a moment.
We know how they get it. You do not know any more about it than we do.

Just be patient. I shall reason with you quietly, and I can bet that within a

short time you will agree with me. It is free, we are told, but who pays for it? The taxpayer.
Contributions.
Yes, but if it is by contribution those who need it most cannot have it.
But they have it whether or not they contribute.

Either it is free to the patient or it is not. If it is not free, the patient may not have the means to make any contribution. If it is free to the patient the burden is so heavy on the shoulders of the taxpayers that very often the revenue of charitable institutions dries up. In England many people who were most generous to charitable institutions in days gone by can no longer contribute, just on account of the heavy burden of taxation caused by all sorts of socialist measures. This is one point of view. When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke he said that according to the American national health insurance board act the destitute should be left to charitable institutions.
That is what the act says.
Well, the charitable institutions live by gifts coming from people who have money.
I said I disagreed with the American plan.

Yes, I know you disagree. The hon. gentleman who is the leader of the socialist party in the house disagrees with that measure because he believes charitable institutions should be supported by the state-
No, no.
-instead of being supported by private individuals.
No, no.
I am very glad my hon. friend has said that.
That is wrong.
Do not say that is small.
I did not say it was small; I said it was wrong.

speechtext:
Order. I would ask hon. members to refrain from interrupting the hon. gentleman who has the floor. That is not in order. Furthermore, if hon. members wish to ask a question they should rise and address the Chair. If the hon. member who is speaking remains on his feet, no other hon. gentleman should ask a question, because only one hon. member should be on his feet at a time.
National Health Insurance

Thank you, Mr. Speaker; but the arduous task for me is not to speak without being interrupted, but to try to convince my hon. friends of the C.C.F. group. That is a very difficult task, but I shall go on with it and hope to make some converts. Then the hon. gentleman mentioned Dr. Skinner. I may be ignorant, but I do not know Dr. Skinner. However, "skinner" is a proper name for some doctors who practise in socialized medicine.
He is in private practice.
I know; but some of them are skinners.
He is not a lawyer, you know; he is a doctor.

If my hon. friend were in trouble I am sure he would find the fees of lawyers most reasonable for services rendered.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to your attention a splendid medical service being rendered in a free-enterprise part of the country, the province of Quebec. I am sorry I have not at hand the report of the provincial department of health, which shows great progress in the care of the people. There is one organization I cannot praise too highly; I refer to the health units which were established in the first place by the Rockefeller Foundation with the assistance of the county councils, and which are now supported by the provincial government. They are doing a marvellous work. When an epidemic breaks out somewhere the whole unit goes to that point, where there may be contagious disease. They vaccinate the children; they inspect the schools; they prevent the spread of the disease, and they are devoted to the poor. They have a dental clinic; they have trucks carrying equipment for the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Those trucks have covered a great deal of territory, and the X-rays have been most useful in warning the people against the-possible danger of tuberculosis. If one leads the reports of the department of health one must wonder at the progress that has been made.
I do not mean that the dominion government is doing nothing. I have a special tribute to pay the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who has given all his time to the study of these highly important social problems. He deserves special praise for that. He has also been open-minded; he invites constructive criticism, and is ready to do all he can to prevent the spread of sickness and disease among our citizens.
There is one man who has rendered, I will not say more service, but as much service to

National Health Insurance the community as any legislator. I am speaking of the general practitioner. I have known many of these men very well and find that they have not only a general knowledge of medicine, but also knowledge, from, personal 'experience, of what I might call applied psychology.
We live in a time of specialization. Everyone who concludes a course at a university thinks that he is a specialist. This applies to all spheres. How many times do we see bright young men who have just come out of college advertise themselves as specialists- heart specialists, ear specialists and specialists on the different parts of the human body. My contention, sir, after conversations with university professors and medical men of great learning, is that no medical man can describe himself as a specialist unless he has had general practice for three years in some centre. The return might not be as good for a young man who goes to a rural area to start the practice of the medical art as it would be if he opened an office in the city where he could describe himself as a specialist, a surgeon or something of that sort.
Some years ago some young students, by means of provincial government support, were enabled to continue their study of medicine. This provincial subsidy was granted to them on the understanding that, upon the conclusion of their medical course, they would practise in a rural area. A very small number of these students lived up to that solemn undertaking. Instead of practising in a rural area many of them commenced to practise in the city in order to make more money. That was unjust, not only to the provincial government but also to the people who were deprived of a doctor's services in these rural areas.
Specialization has gone so far today that everyone wants to go to the hospital, even for a checkup. The hospitals are filled. If anyone hurts his finger, instead of going to a doctor and returning home he stays at the hospital for a few days. Everyone seems to believe that no illness can be cured outside of a hospital. It is for this reason that, even though our hospitals are large, they are not large enough to receive those who really need hospitalization for some major operation. It is not the same as in the old days. Then, everyone would trust his family doctor in a case of ordinary illness. Today if someone suffers from a certain deficiency he has to knock on the door of several specialists.
If someone goes to the hospital for any disability or deficiency, the number of doctors coming to his room is something incredible. A specialist comes for one ear and another specialist for the other ear; one comes for the
[Mr. Pouliot.l

right eye and another for the left eye and the nose. There is no end to it.
Could not the one doctor look after both eyes?

It all depends on the case. In the eyes of some people the outlook for the socialist governments of England and Saskatchewan is desperate.
I have another reason for opposing health insurance in addition to the fact that the people who need it most could not contribute.
They would get it anyhow.

There is a preference for army doctors. Think of all the difficulty I had with army doctors during the war; some of them were good but many others were bad. With that health insurance system we would have the military preference given to army doctors and we would see a lot of quacks and blacksmiths going ahead of very good doctors who had no military service. During the war, Mr. Speaker, you were present when I mentioned the cruelty of army doctors to soldiers. The list was very long. One day I received a letter from the dean of the medical faculty of one of our universities saying that I was unjust to the faculty. I sent him a few copies of Hansard and he replied that it was unfortunate but he expected such things could have happened.
To tell the new members who were not here during the war what was done to the N.R.M.A. personnel and other soldiers by army doctors would take a long time, and the time at my disposal does not permit it. I will mention one series of cases, though. Very often draftees were examined by army doctors and put in category A, while they were suffering from disabilities which would have put them in class E. I had to make representations to the Department of National Defence and to the National War Services department to enable those men to undergo another medical examination by competent doctors. In nine cases out of ten the men who had been put in class A were put into class E after that medical examination. I believe that is sufficient to clearly establish my case. It was enough to establish that the doctors who had examined the N.R.M.A. men or the soldiers were incompetent or completely neglectful while doing their work. Many times mothers wrote to me asking that their sons who were in the army be X-rayed to find out how they were. They did that just for the motherly satisfaction of having their sons well looked after by the medical branch of the army. I received letters from Montreal and Toronto complaining of what I had said. Those who wrote to me had read only summary reports of my speeches. But

when I sent them Hansard with the remarks in full, they changed their minds, realizing that reform was necessary.
I do not see why military preference should apply in favour of any army doctor. I know of one in particular, in the city of Quebec, whose name I have in mind, who was in charge of M.D. No. 5 during the war and who qualified himself for overseas service by a Cook's tour of a month or two over there. Can we say that he is a gallant warrior and that he followed the troops to the battle front when he was somewhere overseas just for a short trip? There were many others like him.
Another reason why I object to state medicine is the fact that every honest, capable and experienced doctor-or at least ninety-nine per cent of them-will become a pure bureaucrat as soon as the insurance scheme is in force. Then to cap it all we shall have half-baked specialists who sometimes are murderers. A young man who completes his university course is not qualified to call himself a specialist in surgery and to practise as such unless he has at least three years of practice as a general practitioner.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke well this afternoon, as he always does. I do not agree with part of what he has said, but I give him credit for raising this question, which is an important one. It is not an easy one. It is a difficult one, and he knows it.
No, it is not.
When my hon. friend has had more experience in parliament he will realize that some things that he finds easy are more difficult than he thinks.
It just wants the will to do it.

Yes, that is the way God created the world; but we are not all so gifted. There is one way to help the poor who are in need of medical assistance, and it is an easy one. It is to put them in the same class as those who receive old age pensions and family allowances, and to try to help them by supplying them with the funds they need to look after themselves at home when they can do it, and when they are willing to do it. Many people are in an unfortunate health condition. In the province of Quebec they need the treatment that would be given to them by the province, and they refuse to accept it because they are unwilling to go to the hospital. There are charitable institutions, but very often they will not go there. They want to stay at home. But they need some assistance and the best assistance we can give them now- and it would not be so expensive after all,
National Health Insurance considering the amounts that are spent by this government for public welfare-would be to supply them with allowances that would permit them to look after themselves properly at home.
I could say a good deal more about the matter because I have been in direct contact with men and women who have quite large families, who have invalids in their families, and who show a great deal of courage in trying to ask as little as possible from the state. They deserve a great deal of admiration. They are fine citizens, but they are handicapped by their disability or by the disability of their children. They would be ready to suffer in silence and to hope for a better future if they had gome assistance from the state in their disability or their physical deficiency.
At the present time, taking for granted that the old and the young are helped by the state, there is a gap there between sixteen years and seventy. At seventy a man is entitled to a pension mostly on account of his age, because it is the main consideration, although the means test enters into the matter. But between sixteen and seventy there is nothing for a disabled individual unless he is blind. There are others who are not blind -there are others who are dwarfed, but who are intelligent and who are good citizens; there are others who are hunchbacked; there are others who suffer from chronic or other disabilities, who are poor and who cannot get the assistance to which they are entitled.
The position of the taxpayer is not at all the same as it was before the war; for obvious reasons, charitable institutions cannot rely so much on private charity as they did before the war. The state must come to the forefront. The government agrees to pay $1,000 for each new bed when the province pays the same amount. This week I had a letter from the mother superior of one of the finest hospitals in the province of Quebec. She thanked me for my offer of that contribution and told me, "I cannot accept because the expenditure for one bed is much more than that." After having obtained some information about it I found that the expenditure for a hospital bed today is between $5,000 and $7,000. I do not say that to depreciate the wonderful work which is done by the department of health, but I tell you, sir, and my colleagues, that one of the quickest ways to come to the relief of the suffering people in Canada who are not blind, and whose ages range from sixteen to seventy, would be to give a grant of so many dollars to each invalid in this country.
I cannot conclude these remarks without mentioning the names of three men in the medical profession in Canada who are most

National Health Insurance deserving. They are all in the province of Quebec. I shall mention the deputy minister, Dr. Jean Gregoire, whom I know very well, and his assistant, Dr. Beaudet, who practised as health unit doctor at Riviere du Loup for many years. They are men of outstanding ability and of great devotion to duty, who have done much for the people of the province of Quebec. There is another name which should be written in golden letters on the scroll of the medical faculty of Canada. It is that of Dr. Groulx, head of the health department of the city of Montreal. What he has done there is marvellous. The minister, and all the doctors who are here, who know about medical accomplishments, will be ready to pay a well deserved tribute to these men who are great Canadians.
My final word is this. I appreciate the sincerity of all my colleagues, but I sincerely invite them to visit any health unit in the province of Quebec, to have an interview with Dr. Groulx, Dr. Jean Gregoire and Dr. Beaudet, Dr. Groulx in Montreal and the others in Quebec city, and I am sure that they will be surprised at the immense progress which has been shown by the medical faculty of Quebec under the system of general practitioners, with very generous aid from the state.

It is not
my intention to enter into a lengthy debate as to the relative merits of the way in which the doctors of this country should exercise their profession. It would of course be impossible for a person entertaining the beliefs of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and myself to come to an agreement on any of these matters. He is a socialist, and believes that the state should intervene in a major portion of human activities, and should even take over and direct many of the professions.
Including law.

Including law. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I did not rise to enter into that debate; but when the hon. gentleman was telling the house of conditions which prevail in England, and was lauding the system of state medicine there, I permitted myself to remind him that socialist Britain was doing these things with the aid of other countries which practise another economy; that it was doing these things with the aid of the United States and of Canada where private enterprise still obtains. The hon. gentleman seemed to think, and in fact said, that my interjection was rather contemptible and my assertion untrue. I am not unduly prone either to complain of what has been said or to explain what I have said in the


house. I am rising now to point out that this is not merely a matter of dentures or eyeglasses; it is a matter of the livelihood, of the standard of living of the people of Britain; and I submit, with documents under my hand, that the standard of living of the people in Britain would have been horribly lowered had it not been for the contributions which went to Britain from this continent. One of the great worries that besets Britain today is the lowering of her standard of living which must inevitably follow the day when the aid which flows from this continent ceases to flow as copiously as it does.
If socialized medicine obtains in Britain it is because the government is able to get from its taxpayers and benefactors moneys sufficient to pay for those services. If, for instance, to make it easy, Canadian wheat were not going to the mills of England at subsidized prices there would not be very much tax available from the British milling industry; that source of revenue would dry up. To that extent it would react against the socialized system of medicine, and to that extent render it impossible.
If it were not going from this country the same thing would apply here.

I am asserting, Mr. Speaker, that whatever may be the divergences of opinion as to the relative merits of one system of government compared with another, socialized medicine is possible in England largely because of the generous and copious assistance that Britain has had from this continent. And this continent, or the governments of the countries of this continent, are not socialistic. They still practise private enterprise.
I am not complaining of what the hon. gentleman said concerning my interjection, but I do insist that if socialist England is able to do certain things which it is doing it is because of the aid and assistance that are going to it as the fruits of private enterprise of this continent.
Explain New Zealand on the same basis.

I do not
wish to extend this debate, but there are certain things which should be said. I am sorry that the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has left the chamber because I wanted to bring some new evidence before the house for his information. I am going to call this exhibit A. This is evidence of what insurance does for me. This is my hospital insurance card. Like all hon. members who come from my province, I can take this card if necessary and go to a hospital in this city

and receive medical services for 60 days at the rate of $6 per day. We can go to any place on this continent and obtain $360 worth of hospital services. The government of our province meets the cost of my hospital insurance. By pooling my premiums with those paid by all the other people in the province I am given protection anywhere in North America.
If I am in Saskatchewan I receive protection for any number of days; it is not limited to 60. I am entitled to any number of X-rays, a special diet if necessary, unlimited care for 365 days in the year if I should fall and break my back or my hip or suffer some other injury or ailment that requires extended treatment. For $25 my family is covered. My husband and I each pay $10 and then $5 is paid for our daughter who is a university student in Manitoba. If she breaks her leg skiing, as she well may,
I know that I will not get a wire asking for money to get her into a hospital. For the $5 that has been paid she would be entitled to 60 days in the best hospital in Winnipeg and receive service at the rate of $6 per day.
Is that $5 per month or $5 per year?

It is $10 per year for me and $5 per year for my daughter, who is still a dependent. That, gentlemen, is the value of insurance. Thank goodness none of my family has needed to use it, but it was a marvellous thing to know that if we did need protection we had it. My husband left today for Saskatchewan by way of the United States because we have no trans-Canada highway. If he is injured in Chicago or Minneapolis or St. Paul or Sarnia he can go to a hospital for 60 days and get $6 worth of protection each day.
It does not come from the United States either.

It does not come from the United States, it comes from the pooled contributions of all the people in Saskatchewan. This plan does not interfere in any way with the charitable institutions, with the Salvation Army homes or with the old folks' homes kept up by various bodies. These charitable institutions no longer have unpaid bills and our hospitals are no longer faced with dreadful deficits because of the treatment given out of the goodness of their hearts.
My husband is the reeve of a municipality. That municipality buys cards for all the indigent people. Everyone knows what used to happen. Some poor old man might have a lingering disease which kept him in the hospital for months and the municipality would be faced with a bill totaling hundreds of
National Health Insurance dollars. You cannot let people die on the streets. If you are an officer of a municipality or of a town council, if you are an alderman or a mayor you must take care of the indigent. The municipality is able to purchase these cards for $10 for their indigent and they know that they are protected. So the municipal people love it and the people who run charitable institutions love it. It does not weaken their efforts in any way; in fact it strengthens them because there are the pooled contributions of all the people in the province behind the scheme. There is a supplementary government contribution but this is the cheapest, simplest, sanest thing we have ever had in our province.
I want to take this opportunity to tell the minister how much I appreciate what he is doing in the field of health. I think very often in our zeal to improve conditions we fail to give credit where credit is due. In spite of the fact that we have not yet achieved health insurance I think the minister deserves a great deal of credit for the imagination and sympathy and initiative he has shown since taking over the portfolio. I am saying what I have said today to try to strengthen his hand, to let him know that we are behind the principle of health insurance because it is the most sensible, reasonable and logical method of tackling the problem of providing medical services.
Let me say to the hon. member for Temis-couata that the reason I am a social democrat is that I have a responsibility to more people than my immediate family. We have managed to take care of our own family, but there are many other families who also need looking after. Not only are there families without resources, but there are many people able to pay for care. This is the simplest method for those people who can pay for what they require. This is the best plan for those who are not indigent, for those who are earning. This is simply the principle of insurance which is one of the soundest developments of this century. This is a reasonable method and we should apply it in a democracy. Wanting this to be under democratic control we use the modern mechanism that society has developed-government. Government is nothing but the instrument that has been developed by civilized man to take care of the needs of the group. Government after all is the most democratic thing there is because it brings to the people the right of choice. Very soon in this dominion we are going to give the people the right to choose in the matter of policy and principle. I am a social democrat because I believe in the right of the people to choose as between parties and policies and principles and governments.

I believe in taking care of all society, not just my own family. Many steps have already been taken and every Canadian province has made tremendous contributions in the field of health. I should like to mention a few of those who have rendered outstanding service to mankind and identify them with the provinces from which they came. We are all familiar with the contribution made by Dr. Banting of Ontario when he gave insulin to the world. We are not quite so familiar with the new vaccine which came out of Quebec. I had the honour last year of listening to an address by the doctor who helped to develop that, but I regret that I have forgotten his name.
Dr. Frappier.

Thank you, sir. He developed this new vaccine, which has been used on thousands of children in Europe, in mass vaccination against tuberculosis. Then in Saskatchewan we have Dr. Ferguson, who developed the tuberculosis services that led the world. Then there is Dr. Stewart of Manitoba, who has given extremely valuable services in the same field. We have the Doctors Robinson of Banff who have made such an outstanding contribution in the field of arthritis-Dr. Robinson senior and his two doctor sons. There are many others who must be nameless.
I want to emphasize again that there is a place for everyone in health insurance. There is a place for the Robinsons in the field of arthritis; there is a place for the Bantings; there is a place for people like our late Dr. Blair, who did so much in Saskatchewan in the field of cancer. Then we have great institutions of healing in our country taking part in the drive for health. At this point I want to pay tribute to the Grey Nuns hospital of Saskatchewan. It became the site of our first cancer clinic, and the facilities of that great institution were made available to the provincial government to establish a diagnostic and treatment centre. It has recently been expanded by a new wing with government assistance. This great Catholic hospital, staffed by the sisters, is now leading Canada in cancer services. I am saying this to point out that the Saskatchewan plan is not a threat to these institutions, and it is not a threat to these doctors. Rather we are organizing the resources of the communities to place at the disposal of the doctors facilities through which they can expand research, treatment, knowledge and the health which should be the birthright of every Canadian.
Give them the opportunity.

In addition to this health insurance card, which is so treasured and so valued, and which I hope will soon be followed in every province of Canada by the same kind of set-up, in our little town we have a new hospital. I am mentioning this merely to add to the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) who I regret is not now in his seat. This hospital fills a long felt need. Up until last year there was no hospital on our railway line between that town and Regina, a little over 100 miles. If you wanted to take someone who was ill to the hospital you had to take a train at five o'clock in the morning. That meant that you came in the night before and stayed in the little country hotel. The person who was in pain had to endure the trip into town, had to stay in a small hotel, and then had to get up at five o'clock in the morning and make a three-hour trip to Regina. The family of the person who was suffering had to find hotel accommodation, which was extremely difficult to procure during the war. They had to stay there, and then take a train back which arrived about eleven o'clock at night, which meant that another stay was necessary in the small hotel. The whole procedure meant days and many dollars to take a loved one to the place where hospital facilities were available.
That went on until just last year. Then, with the assistance of our provincial government, and with the backing of our insurance which now sees that this hospital is properly financed, we built one of twenty-four new hospitals that up to that time had been built in the province in the last four years. When you go into this hospital, as I did on New Year's day, you find happy families in the corridors. The place is crowded with visitors. People come in from the village and from miles around. The wards are full. There is the mother and the new baby; there is the grandfather; there is the child with mumps or measles. There are the facilities for treatment, the trained nurse, the splendid young doctor whom we would never have been able to get without this hospital, because well trained doctors do not go to villages any more unless there is a hospital there.
In this hospital we have proper surgical equipment. We have an emergency operating light so that if the power plant in the village goes off the operation will still go on. We have the most modern kind of operating lamp. We have the most modern kind of incubator which can be plugged into a socket, heated, taken to the country, and brought back with a premature infant.
Where is this?

This is at Kipling. We will never know how many lives that hospital will save. I repeat that it is one of the twenty-four new hospitals that had been built before June of last year. Of course, we are out of the minister's grants. We were too smart; we went too fast, so we get nothing from those grants. That is one of the penalties of leading in the field of health. Those provinces which have not yet started to build hospitals will now come in and receive grants, but we are glad they are doing that. I do not begrudge any hospital aid which may be given, even though we built our own without it.
I repeat, this is the sort of reasonable, sensible thing that sensible people should do, to supply the facilities where skilled people can reach the greatest possible number of patients. The young doctor, whom we have been fortunate enough to get, is a well trained young surgeon who took his post-graduate work in Scotland. He came to look over our proposition, just to make a call, and he has been there ever since. He was so delighted with our hospital, he just stayed.
This is the best protection that mothers and children can have. It is the best protection that families can have. It is the most democratic set-up you could have because the hospital is run by a board that is elected through the rural municipal and village councils which participate in the hospital district. This is a health centre, Mr. Speaker, and this is a unit which the people voted to join. They took a vote in their municipalities. They voted to come in themselves. They decided to do this, they support it, and they administer it through the board that is elected year by year.
What could be more democratic, what could be more useful, what could be more helpful than to cover our land with small hospitals available to rural people, and in these hospitals install the equipment and the facilities that will attract ambitious well-trained young medical men, and well-trained young nurses who wish to do their best in their profession.
Coming back to insurance, I want to exhibit again this card which gives all the people of our province medical services for 365 days a year in the province, and gives us medical care up to $6 per day for sixty days anywhere in North America. I submit this evidence for the benefit of any hon. friend who is still afraid of health insurance.
In closing I want to say that yesterday I had the privilege of reading a report on the world health organization, one of the latest agencies to be established under the United Nations. I was pleased to see that, in the

I think it is a splendid thing that we have men who can go from Canada to lead the world back to health, but I think it is regrettable if we do not lead within Canada, and if we stop short of overall protection of our own people. We are not limited by lack of resources. We are not a poor, decimated, battle-ridden country such as Great Britain, Germany, or other countries of Europe today. We are much richer because of the war.
When people talk about what it has cost us to help Great Britain I think we should at least have the decency to admit how much it has helped us too. Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to tell you that I am very glad I heard such interesting speeches this afternoon. I hope that during the Easter recess you may find a way of letting us hear, from our desks, speeches as interesting as those that were made this afternoon. As I was not in my own seat, I was able to hear the speech of the C.C.F. party leader (Mr. Coldwell), that of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) as well as the remarks of the charming and only lady member of this house (Mrs. Strum), who told us what she thinks of the C.C.F.
I have only a few remarks to make at the present time. I am particularly happy about the level at which this discussion has been taking place. A few days ago I read an article by the former leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Mackenzie King) in which he said that men must come before material things, in other words that human capital must have priority over material things, and that even governments had long neglected the human values to care for only the material values.
Inasmuch as, in my sphere, I have always cared simply for men and not for material things, I was glad when I heard a while ago

National Health Insurance the C.C.F. party leader make a speech which, I must confess, has pleased me.
Now, I have heard a different version from the hon. member for Temiscouata. One cannot arrive at a conclusion by reading only a few pages from a book. But when one reads a whole book and weighs the arguments, it is still exceedingly difficult to arrive at a conclusion, without having had some experience and without sound judgment.
With reference to national health, although I approve in principle the speech made by the leader of the C.C.F. party-and I am speaking for myself as a country doctor- the rural population need the help of medical service.
I have been practising medicine for over 30 years; my father and my grandfather did the same for over 50 years. Therefore, I may state that the rural population-especially the population with which I am acquainted: that of the province of Quebec-is now lacking proper medical care. Many things are lacking in this connection.
I wish to congratulate the Liberal party and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) for what they have done so far for the welfare of the rural population. Health insurance would serve them no purpose at the present time because we have neither the means nor the facilities to take proper care of that population. A great many of my rural patients are presently in need of medical care, hospitalization, X-ray examination, etc., but there are no institutions available and ready to receive them.
The action which the government has taken in having small hospitals built- especially in rural districts-is, to my mind, the beginning of socialized medicine. Undue haste should be avoided, because, as I said, we are unable to give those people the care they need. Even if we now had specialized physicians, the needed institutions are nonexistent. Besides, we lack people with the required ability, especially in the rural areas.
I do not wish to offend country doctors, but neither do I want medicine to be decentralized, as it is seemingly intended. The hon. the Minister of National Health and Welfare should not decentralize specialized services, such as those connected with cancer and tuberculosis. Some latitude might be given as regards the early diagnosis of cases, but when it comes to treatment,
[Mr. Laurendeau.l
especially for cancer, the patients should be sent to specialized institutions. I would not like research to be decentralized or have rural hospitals claim the right to treat all cancer cases. I do not feel this would be of benefit to the patient.
In the matter of grants for the building of rural hospitals, I should like to point out to the minister that in my district, for instance, in centres such as Louisville, Berthierville, St. Gabriel de Brandon, the best plan would be to build small hospitals, in each case with the co-operation of the provincial government. They could be provided with a clinic, a few beds for purposes of general medical practice and even a section for old people, which could also serve as an old folks' home. They should also have an up-to-date laboratory for purposes of diagnosis.
I feel it would be more practical to build a sort of clinic for the aged, maternity cases and general medicine.
Again, I do not think it would be wise to build large hospitals in rural areas because there are not enough specialists and practitioners of major surgery.
I do not think it advisable for you to decentralize medicine to that extent. What makes a good surgeon, a good radiologist, a good biologist, is not only technical knowledge but what has been learned through examinations and operations.
Mr. Speaker, without reflecting any discredit on the rural surgeons, or on small town surgeons, I feel that the welfare of our rural population requires that the practice of specialized medicine be restricted to the large centres.
I sincerely thank the minister for the substantial grants given for research work on cancer, in Montreal, especially for work done at the Radium Institute. He should carry on his efforts in that direction, because there are laboratories, in Montreal and Quebec, located near the hospitals. As a matter of fact, the doctors and surgeons in rural centres have not enough practice, as they are not called to perform a great enough number of major operations. Speaking through experience and as a rural surgeon, I would suggest that small hospitals be built, for various purposes, and that cases of major operations and mental cases be treated in large centres only.

I have in mind, precisely, the hospital of Joliette, a city located near my home town. It is a splendid hospital whose physicians go to New York and Paris to take postgraduate courses, which are surely beneficial to the patients of that institution. Should general medicine be divided into too many spheres, I believe that it would be detrimental to the rural population.
A short while ago, the leader of the C.C.F. spoke about socialized medicine. That is all right and I believe that eventually the government will establish it. However, the time is not yet ripe and I even understand that Canadian doctors are vigorously opposed to it. Although I do not know what results and consequences that method has brought about in England, I submit that there is certainly something to be done in this respect. However, I wish to insist on the fact that our rural people should have the right to be examined free of charge in our hospitals and should have the benefit of X-ray services and laboratory examinations such as urine and blood tests. This would greatly help their family doctors in their diagnosis.
The doctor could indeed direct more safely his patient to a rural hospital or to a large centre according to the seriousness of the case.
I sincerely congratulate the government for what they have done in the district and elsewhere, for doing the utmost to improve our national health.
Without interfering in the differences between the provinces and the dominion-I feel the minister is better qualified than I to deal with this question,-the matter of provincial autonomy is certainly involved, for as we all know national health comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces rather than under that of the dominion. For that reason, I congratulate the government again on the splendid assistance they have given the provinces in that particular field. I quite understand that certain members claim it will be necessary to levy heavy taxes for the purpose of securing free medical aid for our rural population. But I am not now dealing with the financial aspect of the matter. Nevertheless, I consider that our rural population is entitled to the benefits and modern resources of medical science. X-rays should not be the exclusive right of the rich. In my opinion, the farmer, the man who labours the whole year, spends half his time on the land in the summer and the other half, during the winter, in lumber camps, has very limited means.
National Health Insurance However, he should have the right to undergo a medical examination and X-ray, just as much as any other person who has more money. I think that these conditions account for the dissatisfaction of our people who should be entitled to benefit from new discoveries of medical science just like anyone else. Now, as to making medical services available free of charge I leave it to others to decide whether such a plan should be contributory or not. I am not conversant with financial or legal matters. I am only a country doctor, practising in a rural community. I repeat that country folk are honest and proud. They would be very pleased if specialized medical services were easily available as it would prevent them from relying on public assistance. The leader of the C.C.F. party made a fine speech. Listening to him, one feels that what he says sounds well and that he is right. I believe, however, that the government is even more justified in carrying on with its present policy, that is, in gradually supplying us with equipment, hospitals, specialists and technicians before organizing medical services on a wide scale as is urged by the leader of the C.C.F. I do not know how things are in Saskatchewan, but I may say to our political opponents that in the province of Quebec, some of my patients, because there is a shortage of beds, have long been awaiting their turn to be admitted to hospital.
