I therefore consider that the government has been most provident in extending to Quebec, as well as to the other provinces, sufficient funds to provide hospitals with extra beds and to assist them in training specialists, nurses, prominent surgeons, technicians of all ^kinds. I do not hear expressed so often nowadays, Mr. Speaker, the idea that all the brains are to be found in Ottawa. I am glad that idea is being expressed less and less. It is well that everybody should learn that Canadians everywhere have brains, and they are progressive. We do not need to have any central board at Ottawa or anywhere else dictating to the provinces what to do in respect of health or any other thing. All that is necessary is to enable the provinces to discharge their responsibilities, and you will find them prepared to lead out and do their job effectively.
I think the house would also be interested in one or two excerpts from another docu-

National Health Insurance ment called "Hospitalization through co-operation", the Alberta government municipal hospital plan. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) did a service to the house and to the country by giving us an idea of what is being done in Saskatchewan. These excerpts will give us some idea of what is being done in Alberta. I shall quote from a speech by the Hon. Dr. W. W. Cross, minister of health and public welfare.
We have several of our municipal hospital districts that provide free hospitalization to their ratepayers. This is possible in all districts if the elected hospital boards, with the approval of a majority of the ratepayers, decide to make the mill rate property tax, plus provincial government grants, sufficient to cover the whole cost of hospitalization.
There were twenty-one of these hospitals in operation in 1936 and since then the people in various districts have gone ahead in a democratic way, that is by a majority vote of the taxpayers, and established thirty-four more in the last twelve years.
This is by far the best hospitalization scheme in Canada.
I have not the information to enable me to judge the accuracy or the inaccuracy of the statement, but knowing Dr. Cross as I do, I would say that it is probably entirely accurate; certainly it is accurate in accordance with the best information that he has been able to obtain. I continue:
Someone has to pay for hospitalization and the total cost for this service last year in Alberta was $8,057,000, or $9.58 per person.
The department of health paid out of general revenue last year through its various grants and free hospitalization services over $4,300,000.
Twenty-five per cent of the ratepayers in any given area with sufficient population, i.e., 3,000 to 30,000 people, may petition for the establishment of a hospital district, or the councils of the contributing municipal districts may petition the minister. When the proposed district has been approved by the department, a provisional board is then appointed by the contributing councils, consisting of three, five or seven resident ratepayers. The provisional board members hold office until the date of the next regular municipal election, at which time a board is elected by the ratepayers of the hospital district. From then on the hospital is managed by the ratepayers' elected representatives.
The scheme also provides for a patient day rate which is usually $1 or free for the ratepayers, their wives, dependent families and domestic female help residing with them."
In Alberta we already have 7-3 beds per 1,000 of our population, which is the highest hospital bed capacity rate of any province in Canada. This has been made possible mainly through our municipal hospital plan.
Provision is also made in the act whereby persons who are non-ratepayers may receive hospitalization at the $1 per diem rate or less, on purchasing a contract or ticket from the hospital board, the cost of which ranges from $6 to $12 per annum.
Each hospital is owned and controlled by the district and the administration and operation is conducted by their own elected board. Several more districts are being organized this year and with the progress that is being made, it will not be long until
[Mr. Blackmore.j

all our citizens will be able to obtain hospitalization at a per diem rate of their own choice on a democratic basis.
We Social Crediters feel happy about the progress in Alberta up to the present time. When the Social Credit administration took over we were very deeply in debt. Just as soon as the Social Credit administration took over in Alberta the people discovered that they did not have suitable roads. Consequently we have had a tremendous amount of work to do in building roads. And we have had many other responsibilities, Mr. Speaker. In Alberta we have endeavoured to discharge all the responsibilities of the government all across the board in a way comparable to that in which we have discharged public health responsibilities. We have done just that. If our progress has not been any more spectacular than I have indicated, and I think it is very good, then I must say it is because we have had a rather wide field over which to distribute the money which came into our hands; and we have done that.
A further word regarding the administration of health insurance in Canada. The nearer you get the control of people's affairs into the hands of the local communities, the better it is. I favour decentralization in practically every item of government, especially in health, in education and in social services generally, and in a great many other things. I believe that the dominion government should contribute liberally to the support of those services in each and every province for the simple reason that the provinces, with the limited revenue sources at their disposal, are never able to collect enough money to enable them to discharge adequately the responsibilities which are theirs under the British North America Act.
The dominion government has access to sources of revenue far beyond those available to the provinces. Moreover, as I have said so many times in this house, and will now say once more briefly, the dominion government has the control of credit, currency and the banking system of Canada. Therefore it has the power to render available financially the full physical capacity of the dominion. What is physically possible can be made financially possible. The only agency in the Dominion of Canada that has the power to make what is physically possible financially possible is the dominion government. If they will do that, then we shall find that the extent of health services possible in the provinces of Canada is dependent only on our capacity in Canada to produce goods and services-food, clothing, shelter and equipment and trained doctors and all the other necessities which enter into the provision of adequate health services for the

nation. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if the dominion government assumes that responsibility and exercises it, along with its capacity or ability to tax money from the people and then redistributes that money in accordance with the needs of the provinces, we need have no fear that within a reasonably short time Canada will have a health program which will be the pride of all Canadians and the envy of people throughout the world.

subtopic: OTTAWA TRANSPORTATION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill has been reported by the standing committee, and I quite agree with its report. There are two features about this bill in which I am interested. If the national plan to build a capital is adapted to our circumstances I am in favour of it. I am not opposing this particular bill and I expressly said so in the house and in the committee. I intended no criticism of the private ownership that had existed in Ottawa as well as in Toronto. The people interested in those two systems set out to make profits. They risked their money and no doubt substantial profits was their aim.
Private enterprise carried on from 1894 to 1910 but the advent of the motor car interfered with the receipts of electric railway systems throughout the whole continent. The people who put their money into electric cars, omnibuses, and horse cars must have had faith and courage to risk losing their money. I appreciate that the owners of the two local daily newspapers in Ottawa have over the years sought to develop and prepare the way for this particular franchise and venture in public ownership. I should like to pay a word of tribute to the former mayor, Mr. Lewis, who took part in bringing about this agreement. The present mayor, the board of control, the city officials and other officials serving the city of Ottawa worked for this agreement faithfully and well.
Ottawa Transportation Commission
I am glad to see that in drafting this bill they have taken advantage of the experience of the city of Toronto. I was head of that city when a similar state of affairs existed. At one time the street railway system served only a territory about as large as that served by the system here; it served only the older part of the city, not much past Bloor street. The Toronto railway system, which serviced less than half the city, was purchased on September 1, 1921, by arbitration.
I am glad the city of Ottawa has followed what was done in Toronto. The three members of the commission here will be in charge during the most critical time. When the private interests first acquired the franchise in Toronto in 1891 I have no doubt that they were out to make increased profits. They obtained the franchise for the price the city had paid, $1,400,000. The charter was to run for thirty years and would terminate on September 1, 1921, at which time the city would have the right to buy them out. Then they introduced Sunday cars and electric cars. In 1912, 1913 and 1914 they had the support of five newspapers in Toronto in suggesting that they would sell the railway system to the city for $22 million and an old electric light plant for $8 million. The five newspapers, the Star, News, World, Globe and Mail and Empire supported that proposal. If that deal had gone through we would have been so overcapitalized that we would have had to charge a quarter for only two tickets. I am glad that that did not go through.
As the city grew the city itself developed a system of car lines and in time this system covered practically two-thirds of the city. These lines were standard gauge and when the city took over the system they were in the position of being able to service two-thirds of the territory with the lines they already had. I am sorry that the city of Ottawa did not follow the same procedure.
On January 1, 1920, the electors of Toronto voted to purchase the street railway system. At that time we had fifteen different fares. The system was unified with a flat rate to cover the whole city. In 1921 public ownership came into being. At that time I was presented with a voluminous bill about the size of a budget speech. I did not accept it and I wrote a street railway act which covered only a page and a half which contained all the main features of the present bill. I suggested that instead of seven commissioners there should be only three, and that they must also be ratepayers who were residents of the municipality. The number of commissioners was reduced from seven to three. The commission was to have the management, control, operation and maintenance of the

Ottawa Transportation Commission system. Those four words were written into the statute by me. They were to operate independently of the city council, just like any other commission. The city council supplied the capital, but after that the operation of the system was placed entirely in the hands of the three men who were chosen.
In the present case, in my opinion, they have chosen three very capable men, and I hope that they will succeed. In our act, which the people voted on, as they voted here last February, I think it was, the mayor was to be a member of the commission. In the private bills committee of the legislature, where the Ottawa bill was recently, they decided that the mayor should not be on the commission. In the legislature they decided that it would be far better not to have anybody connected with the council on the commission, the same as in the Ottawa bill. No member of the council could be appointed to the commission. It was to be independent of the city council when appointed. They were to have control over the operation of the system, and it was to be run at cost after depreciation and sinking fund charges. That is in the Ottawa bill, too. Not a cent of taxes has ever been collected from the people of Toronto to support the system. It is entirely self-sustaining out of the earnings of the system. Not a cent of taxes has been collected for capital. The car riders pay the entire cost. The commission is appointed for three years. The Toronto act gave the system the right to build subways and operate interurban buses. I hope that Ottawa will follow the same course. If they do I think they will be on safe ground.
I may say that I had some trouble, as they had here in Ottawa, to secure three good men, but I believe we got three good men in the Toronto system. After a lot of trouble with politicians, and so on, I appointed three good men, Mr. P. W. Ellis, Mr. George Wright and Mr. Fred Miller. I chose those three men myself. They were appointed in the morning. The next day council met and gave them two and a half million dollars for capital. After :hree years of operation they paid out of the earnings $23 million, or half the debt which they assumed for the whole system to take it over.
I think that is about all I have to say. We appointed three very good men, and the road was acquired accordingly. As I say, we have had honesty and efficiency in the system. While the commissioners act as a corporation, under the constitution setting forth the purposes the people who are responsible are the three men. Therefore they must be very capable men. I think you have made such appointments here. The Toronto council of 1920 should be remembered for the appointment of the three men whom I chose. The

appointees gave their services for nothing. May I wish the city of Ottawa every success in their new venture. I am sure that, if they follow the cardinal principles that we had in our statute, they will have success in public ownership which will mean the betterment of the welfare of the people as a whole. I am sorry that they did not take this step long ago.

I should like to have the high privilege of associating myself with the remarks of the hon. member for one of the Toronto ridings who has just sat down. It has been my privilege to know what he did in his position as administrator of municipal affairs when he was for seven years mayor of the city of Toronto. I know what he was able to do in a like instance some twenty years ago. It was my pleasure to support him then on the project which he undertook on behalf of the citizens at that time. The words which have come from his lips tonight might well be remembered by our friends in the city of Ottawa. It has been the voice of experience speaking. I know from my own limited association with my hon. friend that during the last twenty years he has done wonderful work for the citizens of Toronto in a similar case. In resuming my seat, all I can say is that Ottawa was twenty years too late in commencing this work.

I take it, Mr. Chairman, that you have called clause 1, and that the schedule to the bill will be passed in toto, that is to say, we have nothing to do with the particular terms of agreement entered into by the city of Ottawa in connection with the acquisition of this railway?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: What is before the committee now is clause 1.

Having had considerable experience in municipal affairs, and knowing something of the problems facing municipal councils today, I should like to join with the members who have preceded me in extending to the city of Ottawa my very best wishes, and my hope that they will succeed under what I consider to be rather difficult circumstances. The purpose of this measure coming before the House of Commons seems to me to be rather unusual inasmuch as municipal governments are controlled in the main by a set of statutes passed by the provincial governments of the provinces in which they are located.
Apparently the terms of agreement were entered into and fixed by the negotiating parties. In the schedule I notice that the property has been acquired for a total of $6 million. We, who probably have not had an opportunity to explore the extent of the system, may consider that is a very exorbitant price, but I do not feel that we are called

upon to determine whether or not it is a good bargain or a bad bargain.
What I am thinking about is that when this bill was introduced some rather disparaging remarks were made about the city of Ottawa and its municipal council. I do not think it would serve any particular purpose to recall statements that were made at that time. I had the good fortune to be associated for many years with members of municipal councils from coast to coast in Canada, and particularly in the province of Ontario, when I was president of the mayors and reeves association of that province. Many of the people who were in the council of the city of Ottawa at that time are still there. There is one whose departure I regret very much, ex-mayor Stanley Lewis, who was secretary of the mayors and reeves association of Ontario, and who was for a period of five years or more president of the Canadian federation of mayors. My experience with these splendid men was that rather than being narrow-minded at all they had an appreciation not only of their own communities but of the welfare of those they were privileged to serve. Before I became a member of parliament I think I came to appreciate Ottawa a great deal more than some of us appreciate this great city today, because here I always found a hearty welcome, a desire to assist me with my problems, and at least a realization that at this first level of government, the municipal government, there was an opportunity to appreciate and understand each other's problems and a will toward national unity not possessed by any other body.
It would be the easiest thing in the world for me to say that I think this is a dilapidated transportation system which has been taken over by the city of Ottawa, but I believe they have moved in the right direction. This is a service which no doubt the citizens of Ottawa appreciate. I know when I want to travel to a given point at a very economical rate I use the Ottawa street railway system, and I am not going to find fault with it. It is so easy to find fault when we do not have to pay the bills. Believe me, the ratepayers of the city of Ottawa are in the same position as all other ratepayers in Canada today; all our municipalities are seeking to provide services for the people with a very limited basis of taxation, which cannot be expanded unless the statutes are changed. The people of Ottawa are going to foot the bill to the extent of over $6 million in order to claim for themselves a transportation system which in the years to come I am sure will be improved as circumstances permit. And the citizens of this city will enjoy the benefit of
Ottawa Transportation Commission any profits that may be earned by this system. So it does seem to me that a transportation system primarily intended for the service of the people within the municipality should quite properly come under public ownership, to be operated by a commission as set forth in the bill, on behalf of the municipality as a whole.
There is one thought I should like to express, however, and I brought this up on more than one occasion while on the executive of the Georgian Bay hydroelectric power commission. I believe all these utilities should pay a portion of the taxes required to maintain the services of the municipality, in order that they may be operated on a competitive basis. In the same way I have said in this house that I believe all dominion government property located in the city of Ottawa should be assessed. Then instead of sending a deputation here to see what kind of handout they are going to receive, they would obtain a fixed amount based on the assessed value of the property, whether it would be forty per cent of that value, fifty per cent or even sixty per cent. There should be some yardstick which would enable municipal councils to draw up their budgets at the beginning of the year and know exactly what revenue they were going to obtain from both public and private bodies within the municipal limits. We have noticed the trend toward crown companies and similar bodies; and the time is coming when we will have to adopt some method to determine what would be an equitable tax rate for public property in relation to private property.
Having said that much, I want to state that this bill meets with my wholehearted approval. I join with the hon. member for Broadview in wishing every success to these public-spirited citizens who are willing to serve on this railway commission without expectation of reward; and I hope that in the very near future they will have a system of which they may be proud, and which everyone will acclaim.

I was a member of the committee which recommended that the grant to Ottawa be increased, and I think I can say without fear of successful contradiction that no one on that committee was more zealous than I on behalf of the people of Ottawa. The record will show the interest I took on that occasion.

Ottawa Transportation Commission Without continuing the controversy that has been stirred up, I must say that at least it appears that I have made the council think they might need some reforms in this city after all; and if I have done that I believe my remarks were well timed and well placed. But if anything was required to vindicate the stand I took in outlining the views of many people in Ottawa, I want to say that in the twenty years I have been coming to Ottawa my fan mail has never been as great as it is now. I have had stacks of letters, most of them saying, "What you said, Mr. Reid is what we have been endeavouring and wanting to say for the past ten or fifteen years." Perhaps I can leave it at that. My advice to the aider-men of this city would be to go out and listen to what the average citizen has to say. I am not a ratepayer of this city, but I have a great interest in it; and I would ask city council: Why does it require twenty men to run a city of from 150,000 to 175,000, when the city of Vancouver, with over 600,000 people, is run decently and well by eight men?
As I say, I am not going to continue the controversy; but I was sorry indeed that instead of using reason in their arguments they resorted to statements concerning a hobby of mine, which had no relation at all to what I had said. That hobby is music; but in their arguments they used noise. I am not opposing the bill. I have as much interest in what goes on in Ottawa as anyone in this house. I have taken a keen interest in the development of the city, but I repeat what I said before, that the streetcars and streetcar tracks are not in keeping with the national capital.

For those of us who have been privileged to enjoy that music through the years it is something more than a hobby; it has become an institution, and I hope the hon. member may continue it for many years.

I do not rise at this time in a desire to impede the passage of this measure in any way, because in my opinion it is definitely a step in the right direction. I fancy the sponsor of the bill would be the first to admit that it is long overdue, and for that reason I think there should be no delay in putting it through the committee. My main reason for rising was to pay a tribute on this very appropriate occasion to my colleague the hon. member for Broadview, who I think occupies an almost unique position in a debate such as this.
I suppose that throughout the years of Canadian municipal history there has been no one who has been more faithful, nor one who has been more effective and successful, in promoting public ownership of this type of municipal utility than the member for Broadview. Throughout the years he has had the great privilege and honour of having his native city endorse those policies of his in a manner which enabled him to establish an unequalled record for length of service to his native municipality. Tributes have been paid to the member for Broadview by his own city and, although I cannot claim the honour of being a Torontonian, I can claim the honour of being at least one of those who reside in what might be called a suburb of that city. That suburb has been served for a great many years by the forms of transportation with the origination of which the member for Broadview had so much to do.
Representing the neighbouring county of Peel I should like to add that we have appreciated his efforts throughout the years.
I take this opportunity of sounding his praise and paying him what I think is a very well-deserved tribute on behalf not only of myself but of the people whom I represent, with whom indirectly he has had so much to do.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48  ENFORCEMENT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house is in a very good humour tonight, so it is too bad the budget is not before us. The purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act so that the responsibility for enforcing the act would rest with the labour relations board. As the matter now stands, if a dispute arises under the present act and after a lot of discussion and the taking of evidence by the board one or the other of the parties to the dispute cannot come to an agreement, the determination of who is in an illegal position under the present act must be made by the courts ovi an application by either the employer or the employee.
I feel, and the group to which I belong feels, that legislation such as this should be enforced by the body that handles the matter, as the national labour relations board does. The labour relations board takes the evidence in the first instance and is in a position to determine which party is in an illegal position or committing an infraction of the act, or, in other words, behaving in a manner that is unreasonable. As such we think they should fix the responsibility on one or other of the parties-the one who in their opinion is guilty. The matter then would merely go to the magistrate's court for fixing the penalties now contained in the act. In view of the fact that you enforce the income tax act and other acts that have to do with the business of government, we think it is only reasonable that a matter as serious as that of labour relations should be handled by
Industrial Relations
those who constitute the court that hears the case in the first instance rather than be passed along to the magistrate's court. Many of the magistrates know nothing about industrial relations and are not in a position to assess even the evidence that goes before the labour relations board. Our amendment suggests that the responsibility for enforcing the act should rest with the government-appointed body that administers the act rather than with the parties to the dispute.

speechtext:
I think it is only fair to say that little legislation of this description was in existence in any country with the possible exception of Australia. It is quite true, notwithstanding opinions to the contrary, that prior to that time the German people had gone into the regulation of labour organizations and trade unions by legislation passed by the state. As hon. members all know, I was always opposed to that kind of policy. The fundamental principle of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act had for its purpose the system of conciliation. If my memory serves me correctly-and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) can probably correct me if I am wrong- that act arose out of a dispute that took place in western Canada affecting the miners. At that time the right hon. member for Glengarry was deputy minister of labour. As a result of that dispute, study was given to a labour-relations bill for the settlement of industrial disputes. I think it can be truthfully said that that legislation was the forerunner of most of the statutes that exist today in the Dominion of Canada. Speaking from my own experience-and I think it is the experience of my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis)-the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act in its day served a useful purpose. The hon. member for Cape Breton South will, I am sure, have a vivid recollection of the part it

Industrial Relations
played-and it was not always successful, of course-in the settlement of disputes affecting miners in the Cape Breton area. With the exception of British Columbia, and to a lesser degree Alberta, that was the only labour legislation that existed in the Dominion of Canada prior to the outbreak of the war.
Out of our war experience, when industrial relations came under the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Labour, through the War Measures Act, we saw the development of legislation which is now on the statute books. Of course there are always two points of view on this legislation. If this bill carries, my hon. friend will, in my judgment, turn the Canadian labour relations board into a court rather than a board composed of the two parties concerned in an industrial dispute. I think it can be agreed that our good friends to the south of us, after the passage of the Wagner act, had a great deal of experience in the method of procedure which my hon. friend would have us adopt in Canada.
In Australia, of course, in a similar way labour courts or arbitration courts were established some years ago, for the adjudication of labour disputes. Those courts are not representative bodies, as we understand them. They are judicial courts established for the arbitration of labour disputes in that commonwealth. I think that any impartial observer will agree-and I have no criticism of what our Australian friends do in this regard-that those courts have not functioned in the manner expected when they were set up. While they are arbitration courts in name, I think it is only fair to say that even at this moment industrial disputes in the commonwealth of Australia are much greater in extent, and occur more often, than those in Canada.
We have a vivid recollection of the study we gave to this problem in the committee, in the house, and across the country, with the representatives of organized labour and employers, on the very matter to which my hon. friend has referred. At that time I think there was almost unanimous agreement that the method of procedure we then adopted would be the best procedure under the circumstances as we understood them, and in the light of experience during the second great war.
