speechtext:
The hour reserved for private and public bills has expired. The house will now revert to its business prior to six o'clock.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that the house go into committee of supply.

I believe now, sir, that we are on the motion to go into committee of supply. During the discussion of this motion this afternoon a number of hon. members rose in their places and expressed their beliefs as to what should be done in the way of health and medical services and so on. A number of hon. members gave information to the house as to what was taking place in their respective areas. I thought it was a very healthy debate in this way. It was the first time that I can remember a debate in this house when so many members from so many different sides of the house rose in their places and boasted about the great amount of good that was being done in this field in their province or area. That is good. When we start to vie with each other for the honour of leading in social services we are actually making of this parliament of Canada something worth while in the interests of the people.
I rose for two reasons, Mr. Speaker. My first reason is this. I should like to make a reply to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). I am sorry he is not in his seat, because during the debate this afternoon when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of our party, was speaking he was dealing with the social services which are at present being undertaken by the British Labour government. The hon. member for Stanstead interrupted the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and pointed out that they were doing this at the expense of the American taxpayers. I do not believe it was a fair statement to make because the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was not
2362	HOUSE OF
National Health Insurance debating where the good things came from. He did say, and I say with him, that we are very glad this continent is able to supply many of the goods required by the people of Great Britain and to help them out. We agree that, if it were not so, then undoubtedly their standard of living would be, using the words of the hon. member for Stanstead, "horribly lower than it is at the present time." But I point out-
He said American and Canadian.

I said North American. I will take American and Canadian as a correction. We could include Mexico in my geography, but I mean what he meant. We agree that if we were not able to supply these goods from these countries then undoubtedly the British standard of living would be lower. But the point to be remembered, the point that the hon. member for Stanstead ought to remember, is that, regardless of where Britain gets her supplies, owing to her present legislation she is making that supply of goods and services available to all of her people. That is an important point to remember when dealing with the matters discussed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I wish our Progressive Conservative friends were as anxious to join in such boasting as we have heard about the accomplishments in the field of health in the different provinces.
My other reason for rising was to do a little boasting myself. I am proud of some of the things my province has done, and I am particularly proud of some of the things that have been done in my region in the southwest part of Saskatchewan. Undoubtedly this region leads the North American continent and the province of Saskatchewan in the matter of health services.
I have the hospital services card which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle mentioned. This cost me $10 for my wife and $10 for myself.
I also have the health region No. 1 card for which I pay $15 for myself and $9 for my wife. With the card from the hospital services I get complete hospitalization when I need it in the province and for 60 days outside the province at the rate of $6 per day.
Does that include drugs?
Some drugs, but not all.
Mental care?
Is the hon. member interested?

If the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is interested in mental care and feels he is slipping over the edge he should come down immediately. I want to say something more about our health region because the set-up is completely democratic. It is set up under legislation of the province of Sas-


katchewan but at that point any influence by the provincial government ceases. There is no imposition of power or authority on our health region. The legislation provides that if the people in the region wish to establish a health region they may do so. A vote was held and 71 per cent of the ratepayers voted in favour of setting up a region.
I am going to give the details of the services we get in addition to what we get under my hospital services card. We get medical care from any doctor within the region who has signed a contract with the regional board, except residents of municipalities 22, 52, 112, 142, 172 and 232, who may attend Medicine Hat clinic. Those are municipalities that range along the Alberta border. The people there have contracts with doctors in Medicine Hat, Alberta, which is nearer to them than Swift Current or other hospital centres. They may go to Medicine Hat and receive exactly the same services from doctors and dentists as they would from those resident in the region or in other places.
Medical care does not include drugs, chiropractic treatment, glasses, serums or appliances. We hope to have these introduced when financial arrangements make it possible. Then we have what are known as referred cases. A doctor may refer a patient to some other doctor outside the region, maybe a doctor in Mexico, in Ottawa, in Vancouver or somewhere else. When a person is referred in such a way he comes under the provisions of the health region constitution. If a patient is duly referred by a contract doctor the region will pay 75 per cent of the account rendered, at the 1938 schedule of fees of the Saskatchewan College of Physicians and Surgeons.
Emergency sickness while on a visit is paid for on the same basis, that is, 75 per cent of the 1938 schedule of fees. For instance, if I were taken sick here in Ottawa I could claim all the attention I would receive from a doctor in our region and he would be paid 75 per cent of the Saskatchewan fees. Then we get out-patient service at the hospital. A person may not be sick enough to go into hospital but his doctor may want him at the hospital for dressings or for certain medicines or for some other purpose. The fee and other costs for that are taken care of. Then we have dental care for children under 16 years of age.
Reference has been made to the splendid things that have been done in other provinces, but I think what I have mentioned should give even a greater lead to the Minister of National Health and Welfare than anything that has been indicated. I know that there is a tendency to believe that our health region plan has limited the freedom of the medical profession. I should like to read

a paragraph from an address given by Mr. Kjorven, the president of our health region, at a district council meeting held in July, 1948, at Gull Lake. I should like to read all of his speech, but as it is quite long I shall quote only one paragraph as follows:
There have been a great many changes in our program and certainly some improvements, since our original meeting of January, 1946, but today I feel that we have reached a point in the regional affairs which marks the turning point between experimentation and financial stability. It gives me pleasure today to tell you that our negotiations with the medical profession of Swift Current for a renewal of contract as of July, 1948, have been successful and, as a result of these negotiations, we can look into the future without fear of heavy deficits cropping up at the end of each year. I hardly think it is necessary to go into detail on the contract, but simply to state that the doctors have agreed to so allocate the amount of money mutually agreed upon for medical care that we cannot overspend our medical budget. I would like to publicly thank the doctors of this region for their co-operation and their willingness to negotiate on hitherto untried grounds.
And again:
The doctors are satisfied that the proposition advanced to them is fair and the regional board is satisfied as to the amount of money involved and the services which will be rendered to the residents of the region under the contract.
An estimate was made by the regional board of how much the doctors' fees should cost. They went to the doctors and said, "Would you as doctors be agreeable to accepting that and allocating it among your members in the region according to the services that they give?" It must be remembered that no medical man is on salary except the radiologist who does work for all the doctors in the region. The general practitioners are free agents who operate their own offices. The patients call on them or they call on the patients, as they would under ordinary circumstances. The proposal was made to them that they accept this lump sum which I think was $481,000. I have the correct figure somewhere and I could find it if necessary, but it is approximately that. The doctors said, "That is fine."
When I spoke about this matter some years ago, I think during the first session of this parliament, the hon. member for Stanstead interjected and said that we would drive all the doctors out of the region. I would quote again from the speech of the president of the region where he said:
We have, at the present time, 33 doctors in the region, an increase of 13 doctors since the region started
That speech was made last July. In two years' time thirteen more doctors had come into the region than were there when we started. As far as I know, not more than one or two doctors have moved out of the
National Health Insurance region. One of them left because he is retiring from his profession. I believe another one left to take a post-graduate course, or follow some other line of activity in his profession.
Shortly before I left home for this session of parliament I was informed that two more doctors were likely to come into the region, that they were investigating the possibilities of a place in which to operate. Therefore you can see that we have not interfered in any way whatsoever with the private life of our doctors.
I want to deal for a moment or two with the matter of complete medical attention. It is recognized by us, and I believe by all other hon. members who spoke this afternoon, that we have not reached the glory of God in complete medical and health services. We know we have many things to do. That is recognized by the region, but we have gone as far as our financial ability will permit. We have received considerable assistance from the province. We have in the region a population of about 48,000 to 50,000 people in slightly over 19,000 family units, ranging from one in a family to seven in a family. We receive from the provincial government a per capita grant of 25 cents. We receive a grant of 50 per cent for all our hospital outpatient costs. We receive 50 per cent of all dental costs, and we also receive 50 per cent of the cost of paying and equipping our radiologist.
There are many things that the people of the region would like to have. I want to quote a short sentence from a speech by the president of that particular region to show how he thinks these things will have to come about. He is dealing in his remarks with some of the requests for extended services. He has this to say:
That, however, I feel is for you to decide.
He is speaking to a meeting of the representatives of the people.
It is not for a centralized committee of any kind, it is for you men right here to know how much the residents of this area can pay by way of taxation to provide services which you deem necessary.
That indicates the completely democratic nature of the organization. Dental treatment we provide for all those up to sixteen years of age. The reason it was organized in that manner is that many of our public-spirited citizens believe that if the children's teeth are cared for until the age of sixteen, a great many of them will never need any expensive dental treatment thereafter. If they reach adult life with good sound teeth it is possible that a great many other potential illnesses will not attack them, and that eventually the

National Health Insurance age limit will be extended and we will be able to give complete dental care to all citizens. It was felt desirable, however, to start with the younger ones and raise a generation with good, sound teeth. To take care of that program we have traveling dentists. With the exception of the radiologist, they are the only salaried or professional men in the region. They are not brought in by press gangs; they are not conscripted from outside. They are advertised for, and they offer their services at a salary. If their qualifications are satisfactory to the region, and the salary is agreeable to them, then they are supplied with dental equipment and a car. Their itineraries are arranged, and they visit these small rural areas and villages, set up their equipment and attend to the children. In that way these dentists are covering everybody in the region as quickly as possible. It has not all been done yet. We grant all that, but we believe that we are at least giving leadership along this line.
I do not want to take a great deal of the time of the house. I know that government members are very anxious that we get on with the supplementary estimates and pass them. They are quite critical because we are taking up time on these matters, but I should like to say to the government that it is their own fault. If they would tell us frankly and honestly when they propose to hold the election, if we are really coming back after Easter and will have an opportunity to deal completely and exhaustively with the main estimates, if the house were convinced that it was going to have all the time that it requires, we probably would not take up the time of the house on the supplementary estimates. Failing assurance from the government that we will have that opportunity, I think the government can expect nothing but an exhaustive examination and study of the supplementary estimates.
I expect that the time I am taking on this matter will be somewhat irksome to our friends of the Progressive Conservative party. They have their claymores sharpened, their knuckle-dusters shined, their arrows pointed and their bows all strung, ready to go out and engage in combat.
Buttons and bows.

Yes, all kinds of things. They want to get at the defence estimates. Apparently they want to resume the next war that they were fighting last night. They will have a little more time, however, to get their ammunition ready because I am going to take more time for the purpose of dealing with another matter. I want to bring this question directly to the attention of the

Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). A year ago it was announced in the house that the government was going to make extensive grants to the provinces for certain specific health services, one of which was a grant of $1,000 for each hospital bed constructed in the provinces. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) mentioned that this afternoon. I want to point out that it is not working as generously as the announcement led us to suppose that it would. I want to read a letter written by the secretary-treasurer of health region No. 1 to the Department of National Health and Welfare. It is dated September 28, 1948, and it deals with the matter to which I have referred. The letter reads:
Sirs:
We have recently been able to give some consideration to the matter of the grants to be made available to the province of Saskatchewan for public health purposes by the dominion government. While we deeply appreciate the benefits which will accrue from the grants, there are several points on which we feel justified in asking that some reconsideration be given.
Under the provisions of the order in council setting up these grants, a grant of $1,000 per bed is made for new hospital construction. However, the regulations to the order in council stipulate that, where a new hospital is built replacing an obsolete hospital, only the actual increase in the number of beds will be available for the purposes of the grant. In our opinion this particular paragraph should be reconsidered.
During the last two years in health region No. 1 several new hospitals have been built, replacing hospitals which, while they served their purpose during the previous twenty-five or thirty years, could not be further considered as hospitals, owing to construction, plumbing and heating defects, and it was found necessary to build completely new hospitals. The equipment in the old hospitals could not be transferred to the new hospitals as most of it was out-dated and could not be repaired to make it of any practical value. The new hospitals had to be completely re-equipped before being opened to the service of the public.
There seems no good reason why all of the beds in these hospitals should not be classed as new beds. We have in mind the case of the Swift Current hospital, a hospital with the rate capacity of forty-nine beds. This hospital is being replaced by a fully modern hospital of one hundred and nine beds. The present hospital is of no particular use and could not possibly continue under the present conditions. The city of Swift Current built this hospital thirty-seven years ago and, while there has been some new equipment purchased, this equipment is not suitable for taking into a modern hospital.
Under the present regulations to the grants program, all that could be expected by way of a grant from the dominion government would be $50,000, and this board feels that the grant should be for all of the new beds, namely, covering one hundred and nine, or $109,000.
We trust that this matter will be taken up with the committee in charge of the disposition of grants, and that a change may be made, making a grant available to all new hospitals, regardless of the fact that the new hospital may be replacing an old hospital.
That is signed by Mr. Stewart Robertson, secretary-treasurer of health region No. 1,

and a copy has been sent to the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. McCuaig) and myself, because our two constituencies are largely in that health region. The point is this. If you have a hospital that has served the purpose but has become obsolete according to modern standards, and want to replace it with a new hospital, then you must deduct $1,000 for every bed supplied by the old hospital. We do not think that is fair. Carried to its illogical conclusion-I was going to say its logical conclusion-as might be done by someone not quite in sympathy with what is being done, this is what could happen. Go back to the old days, when we had railroad camps, logging camps, construction camps and so on, and I have worked in many of them. We had what was called a hospital but was usually referred to as a pest house. If a man got anything from scabies to typhoid fever, smallpox or anything else, he was taken to this little place. Suppose a village still had one of those hospitals, which it had renovated and whitewashed a bit, and then it felt able to build a new hospital, in the expectation of getting this grant. It would find that for each of the old jackpine pole beds in the old pest house, which was passed on from the construction camp to the village which now exists at that spot, $1,000 could be deducted from any grant that might be made.
That is what could happen. Perhaps that is a bit extreme; but under the order in council and regulations it could happen, and it should not be allowed to happen. When a municipality embracing an area both urban and rural undertakes to build a union hospital and taxes its people for that purpose, in the belief that according to an announcement made in this House of Commons they are going to get a grant of $1,000 per bed, that undertaking should be carried out. They set their sights accordingly; they dig their basement; they call for tenders and get all ready to build their new hospital with all modern equipment. Then suddenly they find that the grant they expected is to be reduced by $1,000 for every old bed in the obsolete hospital, and their financial arrangements are knocked cock-eyed, so that in some cases they are not able to go ahead with the construction. In other cases they have to go back and tell their people that as a result of this deduction another mill or two must be added to the property tax. I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to give serious consideration to this aspect of the matter.
I should like to go on with other things, Mr. Speaker. I have a number of very interesting documents in reference to the health region, but I need not take the time
National Health Insurance of the house tonight. I am hoping that what I have said will be accepted by the minister as the truth-not all the facts nor the whole truth, but nothing but the truth-and that this government will undertake to give a lead in order to make services of this kind available all across Canada. Like my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), I do not want to have authority centralized so that people are told, "You must do this thing, and you must not do that thing." I want this central government to make it possible for those areas or provinces that wish to do certain things to carry out their wishes, with certain financial assistance from this government. If they will do that they will find, as the hon. member for Lethbridge has said, that many communities will be able to go ahead with hospital and health services such as are already provided in some portions of the country; and those portions which already have this service will be able to extend it under leadership of that kind provided by the federal government.
If the hon. member will permit a simple question, in the health region he spoke of, with 48,000 or 50,000 people, how many hospital beds are there?
I would have to look up the records. If the hon. member wishes it on Hansard I can give it on another occasion. If he wishes the information privately I shall look it up and give it to him.
I just wondered.
There are so many village hospitals and new union hospitals that I have not been able to keep up to date on the matter, but there has been a considerable increase.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I suppose I may now assume, Mr. Speaker, that we have had a general discussion and that I am expected in closing to say something regarding some of the speeches we have heard today. I cannot be expected, of course, to cover everything that has been said, for instance, in the speech made by the hon. gentleman who just resumed his seat; he would not expect me to deal in detail with his remarks. The particular matter he raised is one that I suggest he be good enough to discuss with me tomorrow, so that we can get the facts and see what may be done under the orders in council as they now exist.
The first thing I would like to say tonight is that I am sure hon. members noted with considerable regret the announcement in the press that the minister of health of Ontario
2366	HOUSE OF
National Health Insurance was taken seriously ill this afternoon and had to be removed from his office. Only last Friday I spent all day with Mr. Kelley discussing matters in connection with the national health plan and the collaboration and co-operation I have received from the minister of health of Ontario, as indeed from all the provinces, prompts me to express the sincere hope that Mr. Kelley may be restored to good health in the near future.
I took special note of the speeches made today by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Laurendeau) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum). I suggest to any hon. members who did not hear them that their speeches are well worth reading, not only because of their content but because of the way these hon. members approached this problem, which goes beyond political boundaries and should excite the interest of every hon. member, regardless of party.
It would not be fair to say, as was said by the hon. gentleman who initiated this discussion, that the present program of the government is one of retreat. That, I take it, was a figure of speech and did not represent his true convictions in the matter. Instead of retreating in this all-important matter of health the policy of the government, while perhaps not developed as rapidly as some would like, nevertheless has been one of constant advance, as is attested to by those able to give neutral judgment in the matter. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to the observations by Dr. Davis of the Kellogg Foundation. Over the dinner hour I have had an opportunity of reading what Dr. Davis said in his article in the Washington Post about Canada's national health program. These are, among others, some of the many things that have already been referred to by the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
There is another statement in that regard which I think bears mention in this debate.
I should say that Dr. Davis is director of the hospital division in perhaps the greatest private foundation of its kind in the world.
I am sure the Kellogg Foundation will be recognized by everyone as one of the great organizations that are promoting health standards and health facilities, not only in the United States but throughout the world. Dr. Davis said:
Canada is outstripping the United States in its planning for an over-all national health program. What Canada is doing is essentially what the national health assembly last May recommended should be done in this nation and what Mr. Oscar R. Ewing, federal security administrator, recommends in his report to President Truman on national health goals for the next ten years . . .
[Mr. Martin.)

I do not know what that gentleman's views are on health insurance, but I take it from that statement, he having been a member of that assembly and that assembly having been the source of the recommendation made to the President of the United States, that he shares the views of Mr. Oscar Ewing with regard to health insurance in that country. In any event his appraisal of our program to date, a neutral appraisal, is one that should be taken, not without full appreciation of its significance because of that gentleman's great experience in this field.
If one wanted another objective appraisal one would simply look at the appraisal made by the director of the health planning commission of the province of Saskatchewan. His appraisal of the national health program was generous and it characterizes what is being attempted as a bold and courageous program that takes into consideration the fact that, under our constitution, health is primarily the responsibility of the provinces. And so that there can be no doubt about it, Mr. Speaker, let me say that by this program the government does not for one moment wish to intervene in matters which primarily belong to the provinces. We do not want to do things that the provinces can do better themselves. We do not want to do anything that individuals can do better themselves. Essentially, this program is one to supplement the existing health services of the provincial governments under whose authority these matters primarily reside under our constitution.
I am sure when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar bears in mind that Dr. Jackson, the former deputy minister of health in the province of Manitoba, was seconded to come to Ottawa a few months ago to take direction of this national health program, he will recognize by that fact that the government was not for one moment retreating from the position it has consistently taken over the years in regard to health insurance. Dr. Jackson is recognized as the outstanding public health official in this country. His record in the province of Manitoba is a record of the promotion of public health; free treatment in necessitous cases with regard to tuberculosis, cancer and the like.
This Dr. Jackson would not agree to direct a program that represented a retreat rather than an advance in the matter of health insurance.
I may say that our program is not a retreat. It is exactly what the Prime Minister said it was when he introduced the program last year on May 14. It represents the first stage in a system of national medical and hospital

care insurance; one based on the jurisdiction that the provinces occupy under the constitution, and on a recognition of the jurisdiction of the federal government under the constitution. The Prime Minister said that the purpose of the grants was to assist the provinces in setting up the machinery which will be necessary to ensure the most effective use of the other health grants now being proposed and in planning the extension of hospital accommodation and the proper organization of hospital and medical care insurance. That was the statement made by the Prime Minister at that time. It corroborates the statement made by the present Prime Minister, who said what must be the position of any federal government in this federal state of ours, that it is up to the people and the government in each province to take the initiative in working out health insurance plans in line with their local conditions and their traditions. Is there anyone who would quarrel with that statement? I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that on reflection anyone who would quarrel with that statement would be contributing more effectively than by any other method he could possibly adopt to the sabotaging of a health insurance system. The health insurance program in Britain was not something that happened the other day. It was not introduced by the present government in the United Kingdom. The present health insurance act in the United Kingdom is the outcome of a continuing process that began in Britain in 1911 under the ministry of Lloyd George.
It was 1913, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No, 1911. The British government began by taking precisely the same steps in regard to local governments as this government took on May 14 with regard to provincial governments.
You are thirty-eight years behind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Someone says we are a long way behind. In some ways that may be true, but in considering the over-all picture of our social security program no one can say we are behind anyone.
Perhaps the minister will admit that in the same speech in 1904 Lloyd George referred to social waste.

Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Asquith and others, early in the beginning of the century laid the ground work, the kind of ground work we are laying today for health insurance. In Saskatchewan the policy of gradualism has been the policy of the provincial government. Except for the Swift Current area
National Health Insurance in Saskatchewan you have not got a full system of health insurance. In most parts of the province you have a system of hospital care insurance. There is an extension of that in the particular area of Swift Curi ent, but the policy of gradualism is the one that has been adopted by the province of Saskatchewan generally. Consequently, I think it is only elementary to suggest that a program of the immensity of the one we are discussing tonight is one that, if it is going to succeed in this country, can succeed only if we respect provincial rights and obligations as outlined in the constitution.
Where would any minister of health be, regardless of his political party, if without preparatory stages, if without a system of grants to meet great needs, he suddenly brought in a broad measure without consideration of the ability of the provinces to carry it into effect. Such a measure would not receive the support either of the people or of the provincial governments; such a scheme would be doomed to failure from the beginning if initiated here in that way by any federal government.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Laurendeau) spoke in French, and I am sure that if the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had been following his French he would have appreciated the points he was making when he said we agree in principle with what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar stated. On behalf of the government I reaffirm the position that was taken by the government when, in 1945, it made certain proposals to the provinces. In 1945 we proposed to the provinces at that time a system of grants for health planning and organization. Those grants were conditioned upon the provinces agreeing to adopt compulsory health insurance. Our position has not changed one bit. I stated that position in this house on February 23 when I said, as reported at page 835 of Hansard:
When this program was announced last year by the then prime minister, it was emphasized that these federal grants "would have the added advantage of being fundamental prerequisites of a nationwide system of health insurance."
That is exactly what the present national health program is. It is a fundamental prerequisite of a nation-wide system of health insurance, and I hope in a moment or two to show how valid that contention is. Then I went on in that statement to say:
Indeed, they represent the first stages. The new services being developed and the new hospitals being built with these federal grants are hastening the moment when in every province it will be possible to consider further action towards hospital and medical care insurance-for which, of course the federal government stands ready to provide assistance. under satisfactory agreements for dominion-provincial co-operation.

National Health Insurance
Surely no one could state the position more clearly than that. Surely that is the position that this government has maintained from the time that it made its proposals in 1945. During the period since that time, on occasion, various members of the government and myself have reiterated this position and I reaffirm it here tonight.
What is the situation in this country? Is there need for preparation? Is there need for a preparatory stage? The answer certainly is: Of course there is. I do not want anything that I say tonight to be taken as criticism of any provincial government in respect of its health administration. We have worked out an arrangement with the nine provinces, and that in itself I believe is no mean achievement. We have the nine provinces of Canada, through their departments of health, co-operating fully with us in the implementation of this program; and as I say, that is no mean achievement in the light of some more recent dominion-provincial relations.
Will the minister permit me to ask a question at this point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes.

To the same degree as the provincial governments help with this problem, will the hon. gentleman, in his capacity as minister of his department, see that the individual institutions receive the same consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes, I certainly will. This program was announced on May 14 last. This house passed the measure at the end of June. A conference was held at once with all the nine provinces in Ottawa. That conference was called for the purpose of discussing ways and means of implementing the program.
At that first meeting I was told by some representatives of some of the provincial governments that their presence was not to be taken at that time as an indication that they were going to accept the national health program. Let it be clearly understood that while eight of the grants were made on a nonmatching basis, the provinces have to put up money, and considerable sums of money, in connection with the hospital construction grant and the cancer grant. I was told by some of the provincial governments, as I say, that their presence was not to be taken at that time as an acknowledgment of their willingness to carry forward, as far as they were concerned, the program that the federal government had initiated. But two months later all provincial governments, speaking through the proper political authority, agreed to collaborate and to co-operate. That cooperation has gone on and continues to go on in such manner as to lead me to suggest that

there is no doubt that this plan will realize the great purpose to which it is dedicated.
Having said all that, I do not want, as I say, anyone to construe anything I am saying as a criticism of existing provincial health services. But the fact is that because of financial incapacity, or for other reasons, all of our provinces do not have the same health facilities. I could take hon. members, if time were available, over a review of the health facilities as one sees them in all of our provinces, and I am sure that such a review would indicate the tremendous achievements that are being effected under this program.
Let mergive an example. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) spoke of the great work that was being done in Saskatchewan at the present time under the provincial government's health policy. I am not saying that there is not much useful work being done; but what I am going to say is that many of the things that he suggested- he mentioned them and properly so-are things that are now being done in the province of Saskatchewan with financial assistance given to that province under this federal plan. Let us take for example the mobile dental clinics to which the hon. gentleman called our attention-those clinics are being projected into areas where there are no dentists. The situation in Saskatchewan is that there is a great shortage of dentists. A great maldistribution of dentists exists in fact throughout the country. One of the ways by which proper and more complete dental treatment can be accorded to the people of that province is by the use of these mobile dental clinics. I forget the exact total because I have not my papers with me, but we have approved at least nine projects for Saskatchewan to enable it to carry on and to extend this program of mobile dental clinics.
Take, for instance, the work that is being done in trying to bring dental care to the school children in Saskatchewan. In Saskatchewan we are providing dental care for over 40,000 school children under an expanded program suggested to us by the government of that province and paid by the federal government. That whole program of prevention and of dental care for the schools, to the extent of the 40,000 children I have mentioned, is being borne entirely by the federal government. I am not saying that for the purpose of trying to encourage this house to pay me or this administration a tribute, or anything of that sort. I merely mention this fact as an indication that, no matter what progress has been made in any province, there is great room for further much-needed advance, which I am sure could not finan-

daily take place but for the assistance now being given by the federal government.
In addition to that dental care, in Saskatchewan immunization will be brought to thousands of children formerly unprotected. I could mention-and I am speaking now from memory-no less than ten hospitals in the province of Saskatchewan which will have improved X-ray facilities as a result of this program. Hon. members will say: That is fine, but what is the point? The point is that there are many preparatory things to be done before all the provinces are in a position to introduce a system of hospital and medical care on an insurance basis that will be efficient and that will not break down in the process of its early operations.
Take the question of mental illness in this country. I am not reflecting on any province when I say this, and I want to affirm at once that in some provinces the mental institutions that they have built are a great tribute to the various governments responsible for the erection of those institutions. I think of the building at Essondale; I think of the building at Whitby, Ontario; I think of that new great institution that is being built at Mont Providence. But I can say this:	there is no
province-I am sure every minister of health will agree with me in this-that can affirm that in its institutions for mental care it has all the equipment that it requires to do an adequate job.
We are purchasing thousands of dollars' worth of all sorts of equipment to go into our mental institutions throughout every province in Canada. Not only are we providing equipment for mental institutions, but we are providing training for psychiatrists, for occupational therapists, two personnel units which are sadly lacking. This lack has a great deal to do with the very serious situation which exists in regard to mental illness in Canada. Let no one think that this is not a serious problem. Over half of the people occupying hospital beds in Canada are people who are suffering from mental illness. Under the new schemes of training and treatment, where proper equipment exists, where adequate professional and junior psychiatric personnel exists, it is possible to effect the most remarkable cures and the most remarkable treatment. I am told by my advisers that in a fully equipped mental institution, where there is sufficient equipment and where there is sufficient personnel, it is possible within the course of a year to discharge over 75 per cent of the persons in those institutions, and of that 75 per cent it is said but 25 per cent ever have to return to the institution. That was not so twenty years ago; it was not so ten years ago. But because of new treatment methods, because of new equipment, it is
National Health Insurance possible to effect what I believe to be a very great achievement in mental health care.
Our mental hospitals have not got that equipment. In the maritime provinces, in the western provinces, in all of our provinces, that is the case. About a month ago with two other hon. members of this house and the minister of health of Ontario I was taken on a tour of certain mental institutions in Ontario. I am sure that the minister of health of that province would be the first to admit that the equipment required, the program of training of occupational therapists required, the program of recreational therapy that is required in those institutions which we visited is so great as clearly to cause one to be very hesitant about making any final judgments about the moment and the time when it will be possible for all the provinces to introduce schemes not only of hospital but of medical care insurance. But as I say, these are all first stages.
Hon. members talk about tuberculosis. We have made great progress in tuberculosis care. But the fact is that the problem is still acute. In some provinces the mortality rate is still very high. The only way in which that mortality rate can be reduced is by the building of new hospitals, by the provision of better equipment for X-rays, by both institutional care and pre-institutional care, by providing schemes of rehabilitation both while the patient is in an institution and after he leaves the institution before he goes back to the job of making a living. We are now doing these things, thanks to the national health program. These are part of the preparatory effort that I am talking about, and by giving these examples I am seeking to indicate that we do have to go through these first stages before we can set up an adequate system. Before that time comes, provided the constitutional provisions are observed, it will be possible to make even greater advances not only with regard to one phase of health insurance but with regard to the whole problem of health insurance, hospital and medical.
Take penicillin. Under our venereal disease grant we give penicillin free to the provinces to enable them to cut down the contagious character of this disease. Take streptomycin. I think this does indicate how important this important program has been and is. Streptomycin is a new drug. It is a very costly drug. A year ago one hon. member of this house called me on the telephone and said that one of his constituents was suffering from tuberculosis, and that according to the doctor he was going to die. The doctor had said that that patient could be cured only if streptomycin was administered. But the sanatorium had no funds for the purchase of that expensive drug. We had no provision

National Health Insurance for it in our department, nor did the provincial department concerned have provision for the purchase of drugs in this particular instance. If that situation arose today-and it has arisen in three instances that I know of personally-whether or not the patient could afford it, that drug would be given free. And in two instances of the three of which I have knowledge lives are being saved as a result of our national health program.
The hon. member for London (Mr. Man-ross), who is not in his seat tonight, will I am sure corroborate this. These little examples do illustrate how important this national health program is, and this is the first stage in the realization of the proposal noted by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Take another example. A woman in the city of Woodstock had had one leg amputated. Her doctor, a well-known and respected doctor in the town, advised her husband that if streptomycin could be applied he could save her other leg from being amputated. The total cost of that drug in the circumstances indicated by the doctor would have been $580. The husband in question was an ordinary workingman, working for the corporation of the city, I think. He could not afford to buy the drug. He called me himself on the telephone on Christmas day-with tears in his eyes, I suspect. He said, "What kind of a country is this that an ordinary workingman with a wife about to lose a limb cannot get this effective drug?" He asked, was it not possible to find some way by which that kind of situation could be corrected. I was able to say to that gentleman that, under the national health program, funds had been given to the province of Ontario to enable that government to provide streptomycin in such cases free. In that particular case streptomycin was applied and the woman's other limb was saved. I feel that that one example-and there are many others that I could recite-is a clear indication of the purposes covered by the national health program.
We are making a real advance through this program. It is the first stage and, whatever be the ultimate character of future developments, let me say, speaking for those on this side, we want to see preserved the traditional relationship between doctor and patient.
No scheme of health insurance will work, especially in a confederation like this where the initial jurisdiction over health resides with the provinces, unless there is co-operation by the provinces, unless there is co-operation by the medical profession, by the nursing profession, by the dental profession and by all other bodies concerned. It is in that spirit


that we have approached this problem. We do enjoy now a great measure of co-operation by the provinces, by the medical profession, by the dental profession and by the nursing profession. I am sure that in approaching this problem responsibly, as we are going to approach it, by maintaining that kind of collaboration, we will have laid the foundation for a more successful operation of the ultimate scheme than would otherwise be the case.
When the moment will have arrived to initiate such a scheme by any particular province, along with contributions to be made by the central government, will be a matter to be determined in the light of the progress we have made with regard to the effective use to be made of the grants of money provided to the provinces. Already we have made a tremendous advance in hospital construction. We have set for ourselves an effort of 40,000 hospital beds in the next five years. A month ago I told the house that within a period of less than seven months we had committed ourselves to the payment of funds for the construction of 13,000 additional hospital beds. I take it that the committee generally will recognize that that in itself is a remarkable bit of progress.
With progress carried on on that accelerated basis the time will come when we will be able to say that there are hazards to human welfare that only the collective strength of the community can overcome. We have seen the growth in this country of the humanitarian conviction that no Canadian should be debarred from adequate health care because of a mere lack of money.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in his closing words stated a proposition with which no hon. member of this committee will disagree. In his remarks he has emphasized some of the problems which, as he correctly pointed out, must be dealt with under our constitution by the dominion and provincial governments. On more than one occasion during his remarks he emphasized the fact that the ground work has not yet been fully laid for the carrying into effect of general plans for the health measures that were first brought under discussion in August, 1945, and that were discussed during the succeeding months until May, 1946, when the conference which was discussing them adjourned. Since that time certain steps have been taken which undoubtedly have advanced the further examination of this subject. Undoubtedly the plans made for assistance to hospital construction have encouraged the expansion of

construction and have made it possible to begin the construction of hospitals which had not already been started.
The scope of the subjects referred to by the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated to some slight degree the broad scope of the problem which must be dealt with and solved through the joint action and co-operation of the official representatives of the various governments. The points the minister touched upon were only a few of the many which must be under consideration in the broad field. However, it would be well to remember that the point now being discussed is merely the preliminary stage of the broad plans for health and social security measures which were under discussion from August, 1945, until May, 1946, when the representatives of all the governments were meeting in conference.
I think it should be remembered that practical attempts, or I shall go further and say that a practical beginning, had been made in working out the details of this problem. Those who attended the meetings of that conference will recall-I should like to emphasize this point-that the representatives of every provincial government agreed in principle with the health and social security program under discussion in August, 1945. It was then pointed out that there were many things about which there was not sufficient information and the first stage was the setting up of a dominion-provincial co-ordinating committee which was made up of representatives of all the governments. The record is quite clear that the intention and the desire was that this would become a continuing committee made up of the heads of the dominion and provincial governments or their representatives, to meet from time to time to discuss ways and means of working out the plans about which there had been agreement in principle.
When the representatives of the governments met again in November, 1945, after the preliminary adjournment during which certain inquiries were to be made, it was recognized that there was not sufficient information in regard to the financial aspects of many of these problems and that if there was to be agreement among the governments which would make it possible to carry forward these broad plans for health and social security, extended statistical details would be required. Therefore, at the meeting in November, 1945, a second committee, a very important committee, was set up, known as the dominion-provincial economic committee. That committee was made up of economic representatives of all the governments and it met continuously from the time it was appointed 29087-150
National Health Insurance until the governments met again in the latter part of January, 1946.
In the meantime they had worked out many statistical details which were of great assistance in considering the way in which this measure of co-operation on a practical basis could be extended. That committee continued to carry on its work, and was still an operative committee at the time the conference last met on May 3, 1946, as was also the dominion-provincial co-ordinating committee. May I repeat that not only in August, 1945, but at all subsequent meetings, as the record shows, there was agreement in principle that these broad health and social security measures should be carried out so that there would be an even standard of health and social security measures for all the people of Canada, no matter where they lived and what their circumstances might be.
What became very clear at the last meetings of the conference in April and May of 1946 was that the details, not only in regard to the financial requirements, but also the statistical details in regard to the hospital bed requirements, in regard to the adequacy of equipment of the various institutions throughout the country, and all similar details, had not yet been fully accumulated. That was agreed by every government, and the representatives of those governments. Therefore there was a request, and it was made by several of those present, that the work should proceed, and proceed continuously and vigorously, by way of an examination of the whole problem and thus lay the foundation for the extension of these health and social security measures upon which all governments were agreed in principle, even as I am sure they are now. The very nature of these discussions is evidenced by the last paragraph of my closing statement to that conference on May 3. We had dealt with the health program and the approval of these principles, and this was the closing paragraph of my remarks:
The dominion government knows the needs of the provinces. It knows where the heaviest fields of tax responsibilities lie. It has had the figures from the submissions of the provinces and from the calculations of the economic committee. I strongly urge that the dominion government observe the remarks made by the Minister of Finance yesterday that you could not quickly make decisions on these things. Decide how long it will take to revise your position in the light of the clearly stated position of the provinces, then call us together to consider a transitional tax agreement which will deal only with the transitional tax problem and leave us free to consider as separate problems other matters upon which we all agree in principle but in regard to which neither the dominion government nor any other government has the essential statistics. In that way there is still hope in the interests of unity, in the interests of carrying out the objective of this conference. I do urge you to carry out that suggestion.

National Health Insurance
Those were the closing words of my statement at that time. May I repeat those words which indicated quite clearly that all provinces had agreed. I said.
. . . upon which we all agree in principle but in regard to which neither the dominion government nor any other government has the essential statistics.
Remember that we are told now that it is not possible yet to proceed with these things because a sufficient examination has not yet been made. It was in relation to a statement, almost exactly in the same terms, made by the Minister of Finance on May 3, 1946, that I said:
I strongly urge that the dominion government observe the remarks made by the Minister of Finance yesterday that you could not quickly make decisions on these things.
What the provinces were urging then was that we should proceed to examine the details, and with those essential details proceed with these broad humanitarian measures about which there was not a single dissenting voice from the representatives of any government in Canada.
Let me remind hon. members, however, that it is not enough to work out the statistical requirements as to the operation of such health measures as may be put into effect. It is not sufficient that we know with complete exactness how many hospital beds there should be, what facilities there are to care for tuberculosis, to care for the various arthritic and pulmonary diseases, how many beds there should be for surgical requirements or for ordinary medical requirements, or what particular type of equipment is required to meet the demands of particular ailments. It is not enough to have all that statistical information. It is not even enough to know exactly how many doctors, nurses and supporting staff are required to man these vitally important institutions.
It is also necessary to work out a basis upon which these governments can then carry out their joint responsibilities in the field covered by that great undertaking. No matter how perfect any plan may be for health and social security measures-and in this case we are dealing particularly with health measures which in some respects dovetail into certain of the social security measures-no government is able to go ahead until there has been a definition of the field of authority and responsibility, and until there has been an agreement as to how the obligations are to be carried out. That has been the essential requirement ever since the conference was adjourned on the motion of the dominion government on May 3, 1946. It will continue to be the essential requirement until the dominion government reconvenes that conference.

It is so easy to make the cynical remark that there is no use calling a conference together when an election is pending. If that attitude were taken no conference could ever be held, because there is never a time in this country when, with a dominion government and now ten provincial governments, it may not be possible that one of those governments, or more than one, will have an election. That excuse simply does not hold water.
We have had some mention of the Potsdam agreement in relation to another subject which has been under discussion. They did not call off the Potsdam conference because there was an election in Great Britain. The election went on, the representatives changed, and for good or ill the conference went ahead and reached its conclusions. So it is with any of these great conferences. Even if there is an election in the offing, there is no reason why the Prime Minister of Canada should not be at the commonwealth conference which is meeting so soon. All these conferences can and should be carried on according to the needs of the conferences, not according to the political winds which may blow one way or the other at a particular time.
But there is another step that could be taken, even if the government has come to the conclusion that it has no chance of being returned here. A great deal can be done so that the government formed after the election will be able to carry on, and that is by reviving those two committees which were set up and were intended to continue as operating committees. There is no reason why the dominion-provincial co-ordinating committee could not be called together tomorrow, on notice sent out by the dominion government; and there is no reason why the dominion-provincial economic committee could not be reconvened through notice sent out by the dominion government tomorrow. Those committees could be instructed that it is the desire of all governments to have all essential facts, not only in relation to health and related requirements, examined in fullest detail, and also that they examine how those plans may be carried out by an appropriate allocation of taxing powers as between the different governments.
Let me give an illustration of how important it is that there be adequate provision and allocation of taxing powers. I want to join with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in expressing pleasure that an agreement has been worked out in regard to the physical fitness program, which he mentioned this afternoon. In spite of many things said here from time to time,

often in ignorance of the details, I know, rather than with any intention of misleading, there has been a great measure of agreement between the dominion and all provincial governments in many fields. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) knows the extraordinary degree of co-operation that existed between the dominion and provincial governments in regard to the educational programs associated with the rehabilitation of the members of our armed forces. The minister knows that under agreements between the governments, Ontario and the other provinces handled the whole educational program involved in the rehabilitation of the veterans of the last war; and it was carried out with satisfaction not only to the governments themselves but, I am sure, with satisfaction also to the veterans who obtained that training. There have been many fields of agreement. Where there has been a desire to work in a spirit of co-operation as between the governments, that has not been found difficult.
In the particular case I have mentioned, it has now transpired that the very extensive physical fitness program of the province of Ontario is working in with the efforts being made by the dominion government. But when we express approval of what has happened it is essential that we keep things in proportion so we may understand how vitally necessary it is that the provincial governments have taxing resources adequate to carry out these plans. This afternoon the minister pointed out the great advantages of physical fitness training and what it means in laying the foundation for the structure of our country; and in nothing could I agree with him more completely. The best way to begin a health program is by building the physical stamina of our youth; and the accomplishments in this connection are very satisfactory. I want to express most emphatically my very warm sentiments toward the Ontario minister of health, Mr. Russell Kelley, who has shown such friendly co-operation with the federal minister in this matter. I want to express also, perhaps with a sense of more intimate concern than anyone else here, for obvious reasons, my great concern about the news that this afternoon he had suffered a heart attack. I just want to say- and this applies to all who assume the responsibilities of public office, whatever the field may be-that all too often in this way we see evidence of the very heavy burdens that fall upon those in public life, and I know I am uttering the sentiments of every hon. member when I express the hope that this vigorous, genial and efficient public servant may have suffered only a slight attack, and will soon be on his feet again.

I was pointing out that in the case of physical fitness there is a very extensive program under way in Ontario; and the agreement which has been reached is between the federal minister of health and the provincial minister of education. The amount mentioned by the minister this afternoon as the payment to be made by the dominion government from public funds was $74,000. I want to make it very clear that I am not criticizing this amount, which is contributed by the dominion government under this plan. But may I remind hon. members, so they will realize the obligations of the provincial governments, that this year the cost to the provincial government of its physical fitness program is not $74,000, to match the federal contribution, but instead $682,000. And I would point out also that this $682,000 is only the amount set aside for the physical fitness program which has been in operation in Ontario for some years. In addition the government of that province is spending millions of dollars on a physical fitness program in the schools, out of funds not specifically segregated for that purpose. So the expenditure on the part of the province runs into millions of dollars, as against a contribution of $74,000 in this case by the dominion government.
That is important. I am not mentioning it to belittle in any way what has been done, or to minimize the desirability of co-operation. I am mentioning these figures to indicate that if these programs are to be carried out it is absolutely necessary that along with agreement as to what the program will be there must also be agreement as to how the funds are to be raised to provide the money necessary to carry it out.
That applies equally in the case of hospitalization, of course. I could point out that under this very desirable policy the dominion government is contributing $1,000 per bed, but that this government was only following the example given some time before by the Ontario government, which had been paying $1,000 a bed for all new general hospital construction, and $2,000 a bed in the case of hospitals for chronic cases.

The contribution by the dominion government in that case is $1,500, and $2,000 by the Ontario government; and those contributions were made for some time before the dominion government entered that field. The point I am making is that these contributions that have been made from public funds by the dominion department of health were made and were part and parcel of this program that we had under discussion back in 1946. But again let us remember that, for

National Health Insurance many long years, the Ontario government has been paying from the public funds which it collects very much more in annual payments than are now being contributed by the dominion government to the people of the province of Ontario. That is also true of most provinces in Canada.
All these contributions are important, but they are part and parcel of an over-all plan. That being so, let us recognize it. You will find there was complete agreement in principle, and there is complete agreement in principle now. The minister of health very properly explained to the members of this house that he has found the provinces were ready to agree to enter into a broad plan for which the payments made last year were simply a preliminary stage. He himself has indicated the basic measure of agreement that exists. That being so, may I in all earnestness, urge the minister and the government as a whole to recognize that there are things to be done which could be done even without calling the dominion-provincial conference, important though that would be.
The motions are still on the records. The committees were set up. All the governments, and that means every one of them, approved of these plans in principle. Every one of them supported the motion to set up a co-ordinating committee. Every one of them supported the motion to set up an economic committee. I urge that, since this general measure of approval is indicated, although it is late, that is all the more reason for the government to decide that it will immediately reconvene these committees and instruct them to make a proper inquiry so that we may carry forward this great health program to which all governments have given their approval.
